## About This User Guide

This user guide covers instructions for using and customizing the Custom Compiler product environment, for both CAD managers and designers who use the Schematic Editor and Layout Editor products.

This preface includes the following sections:

- New in This Release
- Related Products, Publications, and Trademarks
- Conventions
- Customer Support
- Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity

## New in This Release

Information about new features, enhancements, and changes, known limitations, and resolved Synopsys Technical Action Requests (STARs) is available in the Custom Compiler Release Notes on the SolvNetPlus site.

## Related Products, Publications, and Trademarks

For additional information about the Custom Compiler tool, see the documentation on the Synopsys SolvNetPlus support site at the following address:

[https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com](https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com/)

You might also want to see the documentation for the following related Synopsys products:

## Conventions

The following conventions are used in Synopsys documentation.

| Convention     | Description                                                              |
|----------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Courier        | Indicates syntax, such as write_file .                                   |
| Courier italic | Indicates a user-defined value in syntax, such as write_file design_list |

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

| Convention   | Description                                                                                                                                                           |
|--------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Courier bold | Indicates user input-text you type verbatim-in examples, such as prompt> write_file top                                                                               |
| Purple       | • Within an example, indicates information of special interest. • Within a command-syntax section, indicates a default, such as include_enclosing = true &#124; false |
| [ ]          | Denotes optional arguments in syntax, such as write_file [-format fmt ]                                                                                               |
| ...          | Indicates that arguments can be repeated as many times as needed, such as pin1 pin2 ... pinN .                                                                        |
| &#124;       | Indicates a choice among alternatives, such as low &#124; medium &#124; high                                                                                          |
| \            | Indicates a continuation of a command line.                                                                                                                           |
| /            | Indicates levels of directory structure.                                                                                                                              |
| Bold         | Indicates a graphical user interface (GUI) element that has an action associated with it.                                                                             |
| Edit > Copy  | Indicates a path to a menu command, such as opening the Edit menu and choosing Copy .                                                                                 |
| Ctrl+C       | Indicates a keyboard combination, such as holding down the Ctrl key and pressing C.                                                                                   |

## Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity

Synopsys is committed to creating an inclusive environment where every employee, customer, and partner feels welcomed. We are reviewing and removing exclusionary language from our products and supporting customer-facing collateral. Our effort also includes internal initiatives to remove biased language from our engineering and working environment, including terms that are embedded in our software and IPs. At the same time, we are working to ensure that our web content and software applications are usable to people of varying abilities. You may still find examples of noninclusive language in our software or documentation as our IPs implement industry-standard specifications that are currently under review to remove exclusionary language.

## Environment Overview

This overview introduces you to the Synopsys Custom Compiler environment. The chapter describes the environment products and explains when to use each product in the various design phases. This chapter also provides an overview of the software user interface and explains how to use Tcl (Tool Command Language) scripts to automate and customize the environment to meet your needs.

This chapter contains the following topics:

- Design Phases and Products to Use
- Software User Interface
- Common Graphical User Interface Operations
- Environment Management
- Custom Compiler Tcl
- Python in the Custom Compiler Environment
- Customization

## Design Phases and Products to Use

The Custom Compiler environment uses visually assisted automation technologies to accelerate custom design tasks, reduce iterations, and enable reuse. In addition to an open architecture, the Custom Compiler environment bridges the gap between digital and custom design.

Table 1 lists the integrated circuit (IC) design phases and the Custom Compiler product to use at each design phase. For information about packaging designs, see IC Packaging Designs in the Custom Compiler Environment.

<!-- image -->

| Design Phase            | Product                                                     | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Schematic Entry         | Schematic Editor                                            | Begin a design by placing and connecting its components in a schematic. Edit properties of components, add pins to define block interfaces for hierarchical designs, and verify the design for electrical and semantic correctness. In addition, text views (Verilog, VHDL) are supported through the Text Editor for language-based design and reuse. See the Custom Compiler Schematic Editor and Text Editor User Guide for instructions.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Simulation and Analysis | PrimeWave Design Environment                                | After schematic entry, you can generate a netlist and simulate the circuit. Perform netlisting from the Home tab using Export > Netlist . Use the PrimeWave Design Environment to define and work in a custom environment for netlisting, simulation, and plotting and viewing waveforms. From the PrimeWave Design Environment, you can also use the PrimeSim Continuum tools for circuit simulation and analysis. See the PrimeWave Design Environment User Guide for instructions. To perform only basic netlisting and simulation, see Exporting Design Data in Netlist Format for instructions.                                                                                             |
| Layout                  | Schematic Driven Layout (SDL) Symbolic Editor Layout Editor | After analysis, you can generate and develop the layout using the Schematic Driven Layout (SDL), the Symbolic Editor (SED), and the Layout Editor. The SDL product generates a design layout from a schematic. The SED product places multiple devices into a layout for device-level floorplanning that meets DRC requirements. The Layout Editor lets you further develop the design. See the Custom Compiler SDL and Visually Assisted Automation Guide for details. See the Custom Compiler Symbolic Editor User Guide for details. You can also use the Layout Editor to develop the layout. See the Custom Compiler Layout Editor User Guide for Creating and Editing Objects for details. |

Table 1 Design Phases and Products

<!-- image -->

Table 1 Design Phases and Products (Continued)

| Design Phase           | Product                                                                                        | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Routing                | Layout Editor Custom Router                                                                    | You can use the Layout Editor to create interconnects (or routes) manually. See the Custom Compiler Layout Editor User Guide for Connecting Objects for details. You can use the Custom Router to create interconnects (or routes) automatically or interactively for digital and mixed-signal nets at all levels of the chip design. For digital IC designs, you can pre-route sensitive nets using a set of custom routing options and continue with the Fusion Compiler, IC Compiler II, or IC Compiler tool to complete the physical implementation. You can also use the Custom Router to add shielding during the routing process or post route. You can choose from different shielding styles. In addition, you can set up shields such that they are shared between two adjacent signal routes. See the Custom Compiler Custom Router User Guide for details.                  |
| Co-Design              | 3DIC Compiler Fusion Compiler tool IC Compiler II tool IC Compiler Custom Compiler Environment | You can open Fusion Compiler, IC Compiler II, or IC Compiler designs in the Custom Compiler environment for digital and analog co-design flows. For example, you can use Custom Compiler products to design analog nets in a digital context, creating pre-routes before place-and-route. Then you can run place-and-route using the digital tool within the Custom Compiler environment. If the design was created in the Fusion Compiler, IC Compiler II, or IC Compiler tool, you can open the design in the Custom Compiler environment to add analog components. You can also import digital DRC errors into the Custom Compiler environment. See the Custom Compiler and Fusion Compiler Co-design Assistant User Guide , Custom Compiler and IC Compiler II Co-design Assistant User Guide , or Custom Compiler and IC Compiler Co-design Assistant User Guide for instructions. |
| In-Design Error Checks | Layout Editor                                                                                  | While you are creating and editing the design, you can use the available in-design features to check for and correct design violations. • DRD tool : Interactively checks for violations in the entire design or in the viewport of your design. • Via Checker : Checks for missing or suboptimal vias in your design. • Metal Density Analyzer : Checks the metal density of your design by layer or by groups that you define. • Color Decomposition Automation : Automates the process in which colorable shapes across the hierarchy are assigned colors for multiple patterning. See the Custom Compiler Design Checking and Physical                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

See the Custom Compiler Design Checking and Physical Verification User Guide for instructions.

<!-- image -->

Table 1 Design Phases and Products (Continued)

| Design Phase                        | Product                                                                                       | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|-------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| In-Design Electrical Checks         | EM Reporter Resistance Reporter Capacitance Reporter Voltage-Anno tation Tools Shield Checker | A variety of electrical tools are available to permit you to check for integrated circuit performance and reliability issues during the design development process. Catching the issues early in the design phase can save time and mitigate costly iterations at the backend of the design cycle. See About Electrical Checking and Reporting for descriptions of the available electrical tools.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Physical Verification               | Synopsys IC Validator Synopsys Hercules Siemens® Calibre® platform StarRC Custom Job          | After you generate and develop the layout, you can verify that the layout was correctly designed by running design rule checking (DRC) and layout versus schematic (LVS) processes. You can choose from several DRC and LVS products integrated with the Custom Compiler environment. After DRC and LVS processing, you can perform layout parasitic extraction (LPE). Note: The DRC and LVS results must be error-free to perform parasitic extraction. Use the StarRC product and your LVS results to perform extraction. See the Custom Compiler Design Checking and Physical Verification User Guide for instructions. Physical verification also includes electrical checks. For information about checking and reporting electromigration, resistance, and shield coverage, see the Tools to Use for Electrical Checking and Reporting. |
| Post-Layout Simulation and Analysis | PrimeWave Design Environment                                                                  | After layout parasitic extraction, you can perform post-layout simulation. See the PrimeWave Design Environment User Guide for instructions.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

## Tabs

The Console tab contains subtabs that categorize the following information: session log, history of executed commands and preferences, and error messages.

<!-- image -->

The Output tab displays the Custom Compiler session log, which includes the following:

- Commands you typed in the command input text box.
- Output from running the commands that you typed in the command input text box.
- Error, warning, and information messages that result from running the commands.

Tabs

<!-- image -->

The History tab shows only executed Custom Compiler commands and Tcl expressions in individual rows. The tab is populated with the contents of the .history file, which includes all commands executed in this session, including those that occur as a result of GUI inputs, such as mouse clicks, menu choices, and shortcut keys.

<!-- image -->

- You can select a row or multiple rows, and click Execute to run the selected commands.
- You can select a row or multiple rows, and click Save Selection As to save the selection to a text file.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The Errors/Warnings tab shows only the error and warning messages that were generated for this particular Custom Compiler session. Errors are displayed in red text, and warnings are displayed in blue text.

<!-- image -->

## Common Graphical User Interface Operations

In the Custom Compiler environment, common graphical user interface operations are applicable across different assistants and other components.

This topic describes the following:

- Pinning and Unpinning Tabs
- Undocking and Docking Assistants

## Pinning and Unpinning Tabs

In the Custom Compiler window, you can pin tabs so that they remain persistent and readily accessible.

<!-- image -->

## Pinning Tabs

You can pin the Library Manager and Review Manager tabs.

To pin a tab:

1. Open the tool, such as the Library Manager.
2. Right-click the tab, and select Pin &lt;tool\_name&gt; .

<!-- image -->

## Unpinning Tabs

You can unpin tabs so that they are no longer accessible when you close them.

To unpin a tab:

- Right-click the pinned tab, and clear the Pin &lt;tool\_name&gt; check box.

## Undocking and Docking Assistants

You can undock assistants to move them to preferred positions in the Custom Compiler window. You can redock the assistants at any time to restore their default positions.

<!-- image -->

## Undocking Assistants

To undock assistants:

1. Click in the assistant pane.

Alternatively, click in the upper border of the assistant pane and drag it, or double-click the upper border of the assistant pane.

2. Move the assistant to its new position.

## Docking Assistants

To dock assistants:

- Click in the assistant pane.

## Freezing Table Columns

When viewing data in tables in the Custom Compiler graphical user interface, you have the option of locking (or freezing) some of the columns so that they remain visible while you scroll horizontally through the remaining columns.

## To freeze table columns:

- Right-click the column heading and choose Freeze .

## Environment Management

You can manage the environment by controlling session settings, creating a custom design work environment, managing display resources, managing the technology used for designs, and importing and exporting design data.

This topic describes the following:

- Session Settings
- Technology Data and Process Constraints
- Display Resources
- Instance Object Parameters
- Design Import and Export Requirements

<!-- image -->

- Job Process Monitoring
- Errors and Event Logs

## Session Settings

You can configure session settings to create a standard startup process and initial design environment for both individual designers and groups.

The available session settings are:

- Environment variables
- General options, for example, cursor double-click speed, the designated text editor, and whether to apply infix mode
- Preferences that predefine input values for dialog box entry fields and design operations
- Preferences that specify whether windows, net selections, viewports, and command settings are synchronized across opened designs.
- Bindings (bindkeys, shortcut keys, key bindings) for shortcuts to keyboard and mouse operations

These are the ways you can control the application of settings:

- You can apply settings at different distribution scopes, from the current working directory to the project site.
- You can apply settings at startup to make them automatically available for every design session.

For details, see Defining Startup Settings and Defining Session Settings.

## Technology Data and Process Constraints

You can manage the technology data and process constraints in design sessions.

Using the Technology Manager, you can:

- Add a technology database.
- Switch the technology referenced by a library to a different technology.
- Import technology data to add a technology database where one did not exist before, or to overwrite or merge imported data by compiling it into an existing technology database.

<!-- image -->

- Export technology data from a library to a new technology file.
- View the process constraints defined in the technology.

For details, see Technology Manager Tool. For more information about supplied technology files, see Technology and Display Resource Files in the Custom Compiler Technology File and Display Resource Reference Manual .

## Display Resources

You can use display resources to determine the visual appearance of a design on different output devices, from monitors to plotters.

Using the Display Resource Editor, you can perform these operations:

- Define visual attributes such as colors, stipples, or line styles
- Define a display packet that represents a set of visual attributes
- Create a packet alias when you want to alter a packet's visual attributes from those listed in the technology file, but not overwrite them
- Load new, save changed, and merge two sets of display resources

For details, see Display Resource Editor Tool. For information about supplied display resource files, see Technology and Display Resource Files in the Custom Compiler Technology File and Display Resource Reference Manual .

## Instance Object Parameters

Parameters are metadata associated with instance objects. Parameters differ from properties in that they can only be associated with instance objects. Additionally, the definition of the parameter cannot be created directly on an instance. Instead, the parameter definitions are inherited from data stored in the instance master's associated cell and library.

You can use the Parameter Definition Editor to access and edit the object parameters. For instructions, see Parameter Definition Editor Tool.

## Design Import and Export Requirements

You can import and export design data in a variety of standard formats.

Import formats and data include:

- IC Compiler format
- GDSII Stream

<!-- image -->

- OASIS
- Library Exchange format (LEF)
- Design Exchange format (DEF)
- Netlist Text

Export formats include:

- IC Compiler format
- GDSII Stream
- OASIS
- Library Exchange format (LEF)
- Design Exchange format (DEF)
- Liberty File
- Netlist

For detailed instructions, see Import and Export.

For information about performing batch translation of design libraries to and from the Synopsys IC Compiler environment, see the Custom Compiler and IC Compiler Co-Design Assistant User Guide for details.

For more information about designing by using both the Custom Compiler environment and the IC Compiler product, see the Custom Compiler and IC Compiler Co-Design Assistant User Guide for details.

## Job Process Monitoring

You can use the Job Monitor Tool to track the progress of running jobs, such as design importing and exporting operations, auto routing operations, and simulation progress.

You can view the process output using one of the following:

- Console Tab's Output tab. You can also use the Errors/Warnings tab to filter output to view errors and warnings.
- Session log file that is stored in the current working directory.
- Text Viewer Tool to display and dynamically update text output for all currently running job processes from the environment.

For processes that change or annotate designs, you can open the design as instructed for that process.

<!-- image -->

## Errors and Event Logs

The Console displays all events and error information. For information about the Console, see Console Tab.

## Custom Compiler Tcl

In addition to the graphical user interface, you can use the Custom Compiler Tcl interpreter to interact with the Custom Compiler environment and your designs.

- Executing Individual Tcl Commands
- Running Tcl Scripts
- Using the Tcl Help Utility

## Executing Individual Tcl Commands

You can execute individual Tcl commands as follows:

- Type the Tcl command in the Console pane or in the command input text box in the Console tab, and then press Enter.

In case you cannot remember the name of the command, you can list the command in the Console, select it, and then click Execute . For details about listing available Tcl commands, see the Custom Compiler Tcl Reference Manual for details.

- To repeat a command from this session, click the History tab at the bottom of the Console tab, select the command from the history list, and click Execute .
- To save a command operation from this session, select it in the history list, click Save Selection As , and choose a Tcl file.

You can also create, register, and use your own Tcl commands. Both CAD support groups and designers can use presentation layer (OPAL) Tcl commands to develop custom user interfaces supporting best-practice design processes. Commands in the Custom Compiler environment gi namespace create custom user interfaces.

<!-- image -->

## Running Tcl Scripts

You can run Tcl scripts to automate Tcl command sequences. You can:

- Create a Tcl script. Open a text file and type the Tcl script.

For information about the Tcl commands and preferences, see the Custom Compiler Tcl Reference Manual for details. To register new Tcl commands, use de::createCommand .

- Source a Tcl script. At the Console prompt, type:

```
source [filePath] <script_name>.tcl
```

You can enter the first few unique characters of the file name, and then press Tab to see the list of all available Tcl scripts in the directory.

After sourcing the Tcl script, you can run it.

- Manually run a Tcl script. At the Console prompt, type:

```
<namespace>::<command>
```

If you are not familiar with the script, open the script file, and find the namespace declared at the top and follow that with the Tcl procedure you want to run.

- Automatically run a Tcl script on startup. Store the script file in one of the startup directories at the distribution scope you prefer.

## Python in the Custom Compiler Environment

You can use the Python programming language in the Custom Compiler environment.

This topic describes the following:

- About Using Python in the Custom Compiler Environment
- How to Run Python Expressions and Scripts

## About Using Python in the Custom Compiler Environment

In the Custom Compiler environment, you can use the Python programming language to interact with designs and create interoperable PCells.

Similar to using the Custom Compiler Tcl, you can run Python commands and scripts to interact with the Custom Compiler environment and your designs. See How to Run Python Expressions and Scripts.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The Custom Compiler environment also supports using Python to specify a set of input values for PCells and instantiate those PCells in any OpenAccess design database. This version of PCells is called PyCells. See Creating Interoperable PCells Using the Python Language.

The supported Python versions for the different applications are as follows:

| Application                                                                                | Python Version                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Python commands and scripts that interact with the Custom Compiler environment and designs | --python311 See How to Run Python Expressions and Scripts.                                                                                                                                                |
| PyCells and user-defined devices (UDDs)                                                    | --python26 (default) You can use a different Python version by specifying the --python<version> argument in the custom_compiler startup command. See Starting Sessions and Setting Environment Variables. |

If you use the SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_PYTHON\_VERSION environment variable or the --python&lt;version&gt; argument when starting the Custom Compiler tool, the setting applies only to PyCells and UDDs. The setting has no effect on the Python used in the Console assistant.

## How to Run Python Expressions and Scripts

You can enter and run Python expressions and scripts using the following:

| Method                                             | See...                                          |
|----------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| Custom Compiler Console assistant                  | Typing Python Commands in the Console assistant |
| Available Python interface for running Tcl scripts | • py::exec • py::eval                           |
| Available Tcl interface for running Python scripts | tcl.eval( )                                     |

The Custom Compiler environment includes oaScript 4.1 so that you can access the OA database using Python. See the py::eval topic in Tcl Interface for Running Python Scripts, Blocks, and Expressions.

- Customize access to process design kits.

## Getting Started

This chapter covers Custom Compiler environment design sessions that describes how to start and end sessions and define settings that apply at startup and apply defined setting at one of several design scopes, from your local directory to an entire project.

## Starting Sessions

You use the custom\_compiler command to start the Custom Compiler tool. This topic describes how to use the command, the command syntax, and the available command arguments.

## About the custom\_compiler Command

The custom\_compiler command starts the Custom Compiler tool and opens a design session. All arguments for the custom\_compiler command are optional. You can specify arguments when you want to start the session with different settings. See custom\_compiler Command Syntax and Arguments.

<!-- image -->

## Starting the Custom Compiler Tool

To start the Custom Compiler tool:

1. In the Linux terminal window, type the following at the command prompt:

```
% custom_compiler &
```

See custom\_compiler Command Syntax and Arguments for the complete syntax and arguments.

The Custom Compiler window opens and displays the Home Tab, which is pinned by default and cannot be closed.

<!-- image -->

2. To set design session settings, see Defining Session Settings.

## custom\_compiler Command Syntax and Arguments

The complete syntax for the custom\_compiler command is as follows:

```
custom_compiler [-help] [-command <string>] [-dynamicThreads <bool>] [-gui <bool>] [-scaleFactor <float>] [-libDefFile <string>]  [-loadAll <bool>] [-localDir <string>]
```

<!-- image -->

-command

<!-- image -->

[-log &lt;string&gt;] [-numThreads &lt;int&gt;] [-replay &lt;string&gt;] [-tcl &lt;string&gt;] [-python&lt;version&gt;] [-readOnly] [-container] [-batch]

## License Queuing

When a license is unavailable for check out, the Custom Compiler tool issues an error message. However, an alternate error-handling strategy is to wait for a license to become available. This feature is known as license queuing and is useful for periodic batch jobs.

With License Queuing, which works in the batch mode ( -batch ):

- The license is allocated to the process that first requests for a license.
- The application periodically polls to verify if the license status indicates successful check out.

## Note:

License queuing is disabled by default in the GUI and non-GUI ( -gui false ) modes.

The GUI mode does not support license queuing.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

To enable license queuing in the non GUI mode, use one of the following methods:

- Use the SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_ENABLE\_LICENSE\_QUEUING environment variable. See Example 1 and Example 2.

Or

- Use the custom\_compiler -batch command.

The following values can be specified with the

```
SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_ENABLE_LICENSE_QUEUING environment variable: 1 , on , true , yes , 0 , off , false , and no .
```

## Example 1 Using SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_ENABLE\_LICENSE\_QUEUING in the csh environment

```
setenv SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_ENABLE_LICENSE_QUEUING TRUE custom_compiler -gui false
```

## Example 2 Using SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_ENABLE\_LICENSE\_QUEUING in the bash environment

```
export SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_ENABLE_LICENSE_QUEUING=1 custom_compiler -gui false
```

For information about the custom\_compiler command, see custom\_compiler Command Syntax and Arguments.

## Ending Sessions

To end a Custom Compiler session, choose one of these options:

- Choose File &gt; Quit from the Home tab to end the session and be prompted to save designs, preferences, bookmarks, and display resource changes.

The Custom Compiler Exit dialog box opens.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

In the Exit dialog box, you can save current settings by choosing Save State and then using the check boxes to save workspaces, recent files, display resources, preferences, and bookmarks.

You can set deExitPromptSave * and deExitSave * Tcl preferences to specify which items the Exit dialog prompts and default Save State options, respectively.

- If a deExitPromptSave&lt;title&gt; * preference is true and the unsaved procedure returns true, the Exit dialog prompts to save &lt;title&gt;. The check box shown is set to the value of the deExitSave * preference.
- If prompting is disabled, via deExitPromptSave *, the tool either discards this state data or automatically saves it, depending on the value of the deExitSave * preference.

For information about the Tcl preferences, see the Custom Compiler Tcl Reference Manual .

- Click X on the Custom Compiler title bar. The Close Tabs warning dialog box opens.

<!-- image -->

Choose Close Tabs to exit Custom Compiler. To prevent the tool from warning you before closing multiple tabs, clear the Warn before closing multiple tabs check box.

- Alternatively, type exit -force true at the Console input line to end the session and discard all edits, bypass the Exit dialog box, and close all windows.

## Defining Startup Settings

Define and apply startup settings to control the work environment for all product users. Use Tcl scripts and environment variables to apply settings at startup. To apply settings effectively, you also need to understand the installed directory structure.

These sections cover:

- Locating Common Files and Startup Directories
- Setting Environment Variables
- Viewing Installed Directories and Files

## Locating Common Files and Startup Directories

The Custom Compiler tool makes use of the following common files:

- display.drf and display.tcl - Can be placed in the current working directory, home directory, or any startup directory.
- lib.defs - Can be placed in the current working directory, home directory, or any startup directory.
- .synopsys\_custom.tcl and .synopsys\_custom.py - Can be placed in the current working directory, home directory, or any startup directory.
- custom\_compiler/init.tcl - Can be placed in any startup directory.

## Note:

The file is not read by standalone PrimeWave, OptoCompiler, or other Custom Infrastructure based applications.

For startup directories, the Custom Compiler tool searches: install, site, project, user, and local directories, in that order .

- Install refers to the auxx directory within the installation directory. To define more installation directories, they can be put in SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_INITPATH (see Table 7).
- Site is optional, but can be specified by setting SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_SITE (see Table 7).
- Project is optional, but can be specified by setting SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_PROJECT (see Table 7).
- User defaults to ~/.synopsys\_custom , but can be changed by setting SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_USER (see Table 7).
- Local defaults to ./synopsys\_custom , but can be changed with the -localDir command-line option (see Table 6) or by setting SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_LOCAL (see Table 7). The Custom Compiler tool writes log files and application settings to this directory.

You can define a file named the same as any file within auxx. For example, if &lt;site&gt;/ layout\_editor/actions.tcl exists, it is sourced after &lt;install&gt;/layout\_editor/ actions.tcl .

<!-- image -->

## Setting Environment Variables

Set environment variables to create a custom environment at startup.

- Statement format for setting an environment variable for csh/tcsh shells:
- Statement format for setting an environment variable for bash/ksh shells:

```
setenv <environment_variable_name> <value>
```

```
export <environment_variable_name>=<value>
```

To specify multiple values, in csh/tcsh shells, separate values with a space ( pathname pathname pathname ). ## Defining Session Settings

Define session settings to control general and specific system behaviors during design sessions. You can control settings for general options used in all sessions, such as the cursor double-click speed. You can control specific settings for only this session, for example, the values you enter in a dialog box for a process you want to run once. You can use the same dialog box settings in future sessions by saving them as dialog box preferences . In addition to dialog box preferences, the system supplies design preferences you can use for nearly every design operation. Use these design preferences by either entering them in the Console, or using them in scripts.

Note that some applications use nti\_shell and pw\_shell for background jobs. The startup files read by these processes is not the same, so you might need to put some customization in multiple files. For examples, see the custom calculator functions as described in the PrimeWave Design Environment Expression Language Reference Manual , Structuring the Custom Calculator Function Code.

These sections cover:

- Setting General Options
- Managing Option Settings from the Home Page
- Saving Dialog Box Settings as Preferences
- Specifying Design Preferences

<!-- image -->

- Synchronizing Design Windows, Viewports, Net Selections, and Commands Across Opened Designs
- Customizing Keyboard Shortcuts

## Saving Option Settings as Preferences

You can save option settings as preferences for use in future design sessions.

To save design options as preferences:

The Save Preferences dialog box opens.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

2. Browse to the required preferences file or type in a new File name .
3. (Optional) To save only changed options, click Save only modified preferences .
4. Click Save .

## Loading Option Settings Saved as Preferences

Load options saved as preferences to use settings from a previous session.

To load options saved as preferences:

1. From the Home page or any design window, choose Options &gt; Load Preferences .

The Load Preferences dialog box opens.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

2. Browse to the required preferences file.
3. Click Open to load the preferences file.

## Saving Dialog Box Settings as Preferences

There are two ways to save dialog box settings as preferences.

- At the Current Location: (controlled by the SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_LOCAL environment variable) At the end of a session, the system offers the option of saving dialog box settings from that session as preferences. If you choose to do this, the system applies these at the local location, which includes your current working directory when you were using the dialog box. At the next session, the system will offer these saved settings when you are working in the same directory.
- At User Scope: (home\_dir.synopsys\_custom.xml) If you want to save dialog box settings as preferences at user scope and greater scopes, you can choose to make the settings the default for that dialog box. The procedure that follows provides instructions for this task.

To save dialog box settings as preferences:

1. Open the dialog box that offers the settings you want to save as defaults.
2. Enter the new settings you want to save.
3. From the Defaults menu (to the right of the Defaults button), choose Set as Defaults .

<!-- image -->

The system localizes and saves preferences in the prefs.xml file at the user scope.

For example, the preferences file that follows is saved at user scope:

~/.synopsys\_custom/prefs.xml

The prefs.xml files are sourced at startup. However, you can choose Options &gt; Load Preferences to load a different set of preferences. (See Loading Option Settings Saved as Preferences).

At session start, the system searches all scopes automatically in the order that follows. Where duplicate preference values are found, the value found at the last searched scope takes precedence. For example, if you have saved a prefs.xml file in your current working directory, its preferences always take precedence.

1. SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_INSTALL (Not available for preference storage)
2. SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_SITE (CAD support designation)
3. SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_PROJECT (CAD support designation)
4. SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_INITPATH (CAD support designation)
5. SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_USER (The default value is &lt;$HOME&gt;/.synopsys\_custom . The prefs.xml file in this location is where your preferences are stored and it is automatically loaded at startup).
6. SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_LOCAL (The default value is &lt;current\_working\_dir&gt;/ synopsys\_custom . In this location is a prefs.xml file that is used to save preferences upon closing the Custom Compiler tool).

## Specifying Design Preferences

While designing, you can use Tcl at the Console input line or in a Tcl script to dynamically apply a value to any design operation. See Console Tab.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

You can specify design preferences that control details of over 2000 design operations.

To specify design preferences:

1. Identify the preference whose value you want to set. The session log file records all settings from your previous session.

For a complete list of available preferences for any Tcl category, see the Custom Compiler Tcl Reference Manual for details.

To display all currently available preferences, you can use this Tcl script:

```
proc listPrefs {{pattern "*"}} { db::createList [db::getAttr name -of [db::getPrefs $pattern]] }
```

In the Tcl script, db::getPrefs returns the collection of preferences, and db::foreach loops through the collection and filters it by attribute.

To use the script, copy it into a text file and execute the script through the Console.

2. Identify the default value for this preference and decide whether to apply a new value.
3. Decide which scope you want the new value to cover.
4. Set a new value using Custom Compiler Tcl db::setPrefValue .

For example, by default, short detection is on in design layouts. To turn off short detection, you can set the value for the preference leDetectShorts to 0 using Tcl in the Console:

```
db::setPrefValue leDetectShorts -value 0 -scope [de::getActiveContext]
```

In this example, db::setPrefValue resets the leDetectShorts preference value from 1 (on by default) to 0 (off) and limits this setting to the scope that includes only the active design in the current layout window. (Leaving out the optional scope argument applies the setting globally).

The setting remains valid when you push the design context into another level of hierarchy, and when you save it for the next session. The default setting applies again when you close this window and open another design layout.

## About the Keyboard Shortcuts in the Custom Compiler Environment

Keyboard shortcuts are keys that you press on the keyboard to quickly access commands or functions without going through menus or clicking buttons in the graphical user interface. Using shortcut keys can enable you to complete certain tasks faster, thus saving time and improving productivity.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Shortcut key information is displayed next to menu command and in the tooltips that appear when you hover over an icon in the Custom Compiler window. In the following examples:

- Shortcut keys for New Window , New Tab , Full Screen , and Hide All are displayed next to the commands.
- The tooltip displays the name of the button and the shortcut key for the button: Z.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

To view the complete set of shortcut keys, see Viewing Keyboard Shortcuts.

You can select one of the following sets of keyboard shortcuts for use in the Custom Compiler environment. See Setting General Options.

- Custom Compiler
- IC Compiler
- Laker
- Maestro

<!-- image -->

The Custom Compiler environment provides a default set of keyboard shortcuts. However, you can create new or modify the existing keyboard shortcuts. See Creating and Editing Keyboard Shortcuts and Creating Keyboard Shortcuts Using Tcl Commands.

## Selecting the Shortcut Key Binding Set

Shortcut keys are bound to commands and buttons. Different sets of shortcut key bindings are available in the Custom Compiler environment to facilitate analog and digital co-design flows or design migrations from third-party tools. This topic describes how to select the shortcut key binding sets to meet your preferences.

## Selecting the Shortcut Key Binding Set Using the Graphical User Interface

To select your preferred shortcut key binding set using the graphical user interface:

1. From the Home tab, choose Options &gt; General .
2. Under Interface options, choose the set from the Binding Set list:
- Custom Compiler
- IC Compiler

<!-- image -->

- Laker
- Maestro

If you created custom binding sets, they would be available in the list.

3. (Optional) To save these settings as general options default settings, choose Defaults &gt; Save and apply the settings to a scope.
4. Click OK .

## See Also

- Defining Session Settings


See the Custom Compiler Tcl Reference Manual for details.

## Viewing Keyboard Shortcuts Using Custom Compiler Tcl Procedures

You can also return binding sets with Tcl to see complete collections of shortcut keys, optionally filtered.

You can use a procedure that outputs the Custom Compiler environment shortcut key collection, filtered by attribute, into a file called bindingFile.txt .

To return the binding set in this manner, use the following Tcl procedure.

```
proc getBindings { } { set binds [gi::getBindings -set "Custom Compiler"] set fileName [open "bindingFile.txt" w] puts $fileName "Binding Set : Custom Compiler" puts $fileName "Total Bind keys defined : [db::getCount $binds]" puts $fileName "\n" db::foreach bind $binds { ## To get different attributes for each binding, use ## db::listAttrs -of $bind puts $fileName "[db::getAttr event           -of $bind] \t \ [db::getAttr action          -of $bind] \t \
```

<!-- image -->

```
[db::getAttr command         -of $bind] \t \ [db::getAttr activeOperation -of $bind] \t \ [db::getAttr activeObject    -of $bind] \t \ [db::getAttr activeTool      -of $bind] \t " } close $fileName }
```

The procedure performs these Tcl operations:

- gi::getBindings returns the Custom Compiler shortcut key collection.
- db::foreach loops through the collection and filters it by attribute.
- db::listAttrs returns the requested attributes for each shortcut key.

Alternatively, return the binding set using the gi::saveBindings command. For example:

1. Type the command:

```
gi::saveBindings -filePath abc.xml 2. Type the executable: exec gedit abc.xml &
```

The Custom Compiler environment provides a set of default keyboard shortcuts. To meet your requirements, you can create new or edit existing keyboard shortcuts. This topic describes how to use the Keyboard Shortcuts dialog box to create and edit keyboard shortcuts.

## Creating Keyboard Shortcuts Using Tcl Commands

Instead of using the graphical user interface, you can create custom keyboard shortcuts. This topic describes how to use Tcl commands to create custom keyboard shortcuts.

## Creating Individual Shortcut Keys

Create individual shortcut keys to offer single keyboard and mouse shortcuts. Use Custom Compiler Tcl to create individual shortcut keys.

To create individual custom shortcut keys:

1. Open the Console .
2. Use the gi::createBinding Tcl command.

The command creates a shortcut key within a binding set (or the active set if one is not specified). For syntax details, type gi::createBinding -help in the Console. For a usage description, see the Custom Compiler Tcl Reference Manual .

In the following example, gi::createBinding binds the keyboard sequence Alt+E to the edit-in-place command.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

```
gi::createBinding -event "Alt-e" -command {ide::descend -inPlace true}
```

In the following example, gi::createBinding binds the 7 key to a toggle operation for switching Infix mode on or off.

```
proc toggleInFix  {} { if {[db::getPrefValue deInFixMode]} { db::setPrefValue deInFixMode -value false } else { db::setPrefValue deInFixMode -value true } } gi::createBinding -event "7"  -command toggleInFix
```

## See Also

- Console Tab

## Creating Binding Sets

Create binding sets to offer a specified selection of bindings to designers.

To create binding sets:

1. Begin by either copying the XML file for an existing binding set and altering it, or creating a new set with shortcut keys you have defined.

To create shortcut keys, see Creating and Editing Keyboard Shortcuts.

2.

3. In the Console , use the Custom Compiler Tcl commands listed in the following table.

Refer to the examples that follow for assistance.

For syntax, execute &lt;command\_name&gt; -help in the Console . For a usage description, see the Custom Compiler Tcl Reference Manual .

| Tcl Command          | Usage                                                   |
|----------------------|---------------------------------------------------------|
| gi::createBindingSet | Creates and returns a new binding set.                  |
| gi::loadBindings     | Loads bindings from an XML file into the specified set. |
| gi::saveBindings     | Saves a collection of bindings to an XML file.          |

## Examples

In this example, gi::createBindingSet creates a new binding set by copying shortcut key definitions from the Custom Compiler set.

```
maestro.xml
```

<!-- image -->

```
gi::createBindingSet "myBindingSet" -from "Custom Compiler" In this example, gi::loadBindings loads shortcut keys from a newBindings.xml file into the Maestro binding set. gi::loadBindings -filePath newBindings.xml -set Maestro In this example, gi::saveBindings saves the shortcut key definitions from the Maestro binding set to a maestro.xml file. gi::saveBindings [gi::getBindings -set Maestro] -filePath \
```

4. After you create the binding set, you can make it available by Selecting the Shortcut Key Binding Set.
