Low Grids

Specifies the starting point information for gridded tracks:

&lt;offset&gt; &lt;lowPoint1&gt; ... &lt;lowPoint n &gt;

The first value is the offset distance for the grid starting points. The subsequent values are the starting points for the grid. Add a character space between the values.

You must select Use Grids before setting this option.

High Grids

Specifies the ending point information for gridded tracks: &lt;offset&gt; &lt;highPoint1&gt; ... &lt;highPoint n &gt;

The first value is the offset distance for the grid ending points. The subsequent values are the ending points for the grid. Add a character space between the values.

You must select Use Grids before setting this option.

Space Left (Non-uniform only)

(Read-only) Displays the amount of space left in the region after adding the tracks you defined. You can use the information to determine if you can add more tracks in the region.

## To create a global track region:

1. From the Track Region menu ( ), choose Create Global Region . The Create Global Track Region dialog box opens.

<!-- image -->

## 2. Set the following:

## Setting

Name

Definition

Flip

## Description

The name of the global track region. You can provide a unique name, or you can use the system-generated unique name.

The track region definition to use to create the global region. The available definitions are specified in the technology. For information, see the Custom Compiler Technology and Display Resource File Reference Manual.

Alternating tiles in the region are flipped. Select the flip pattern:

- Y : Flips alternating tiles in the y-direction only. Start the flips with the second tile in the y-direction.
- X : Flips alternating tiles in the x-direction only. Start the flips with the second tile in the x-direction.
- X First : Start the flips with the first tile in the x-direction.
- Y First : Start the flips with the first tile in the y-direction.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

| Setting     | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Tile Offset | The offset distance of the first tile. The offset distance is calculated using one of the following methods: ◦ Auto : Automatically calculates the offset distance from the bottom-left corner of the PR boundary. ◦ X and Y : Lets you manually specify the X and Y distance between the first tile and the bottom-left corner of the global track region. Track grids on perpendicular tracks should also apply tile offset. For example, grids on vertical tracks should apply tile offset Y. Grids on horizontal tracks should tile offset X. |

3. When you are finished, click Create . The global track region is created.

To view the tracks in the global track region, see Displaying and Hiding Track Regions on the Canvas.

3. Orientation : Specify the orientation of the region. Only R0 , R180 , MX , and MY are the valid values and the default is R0 .

This orientation attribute does not affect the boundary of track region. The tracks are transformed according to the orientation of the track region.

## Note:

- Both Track Region and Global Track Region support Orientation.
- Tiles (and groups) are constructed from right to left and from top to bottom for a R180 region; from right to left and from bottom to up for an MY region; from left to right and from top to bottom for an MX region.
- Tile offset is based on the upper-right/lower-right/upper-left point of the boundary for R180/MY/MX regions respectively (when track offsets are relative to the region boundary).
- The orientation is R0 for an existing track region already created in the design.
4. From : Filter the region definitions from design, technology, or both (technology and design). Valid values are Design , Technology , and All .

## Transaction History Assistant

The Transaction History assistant lists all the command operations that you performed in reverse chronological order. You can use the list to track the operations you performed. You can also use the list to return the design to any previously committed state in this design session.

The Transaction History assistant stores up to 256 command operations per design. When the maximum number of commands is reached, the assistant releases the oldest record so that it can add a new record.

In an edit-in-place context, the Transaction History assistant displays the list of commands of the design that is being edited in place.

The list of commands in the Transaction History assistant is not retained across Custom Compiler sessions. When you close a design, the list in the Transaction History assistant is cleared.

By default, the list of commands in the Transaction History assistant is retained after a Save design operation. To clear the list after a Save design operation, use the deUndoClearOnSave Tcl preference.

- Displaying the Transaction History Assistant
- Using the Transaction History List

<!-- image -->

The Transaction History assistant lists all the command

<!-- image -->

operations that you performed in reverse chronological order. This video tutorial shows how to display the Transaction History assistant and use the Transaction History List to retrace design operations.

## [Displaying the Transaction History Assistant](http://spdocs.synopsys.com/dow_retrieve/latest/training/dg/custom_compiler/CC_transaction_history.mp4)

[To display the Transaction History assistant:](http://spdocs.synopsys.com/dow_retrieve/latest/training/dg/custom_compiler/CC_transaction_history.mp4)

- In any layout, schematic, or symbol view, choose Window &gt; Assistants &gt; Transaction History . The assistant appears on the right side of the window.

If you have already executed commands, those commands are listed in the assistant. Otherwise, the assistant is empty and will begin recording the command operations.

<!-- image -->

If you are using scripts, transactions involving direct calls to the OpenAccess Tcl API are marked with the title "unnamed".

Only operations that change data is recorded as transactions. The process of saving is transparent; saving records no transaction. (The save operation changes the on-disk data, but not the in-memory data).

<!-- image -->

You can use this list to return the design to any previously committed state in this design session.

## Using the Transaction History List

The following table lists the operations you can perform in the Transaction History assistant.

| To:                                                       | Perform this action:                                                                                                                                         |
|-----------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Undo a command operation                                  | Press U. This undoes the transaction.                                                                                                                        |
| Redo a command operation                                  | Press Shift-U. This reexecutes the transaction. You can use the redo operation to step forward through a transaction history sequence one command at a time. |
| Return to a preceding state                               | Select the transaction after it.                                                                                                                             |
| Jump to a later state                                     | Select a later transaction.                                                                                                                                  |
| Take design development in a new direction from any state | Jump to that state, and then execute new commands. (Caution: The system erases all succeeding transactions from the previous history list).                  |
| Save a version of the design that matches a state         | Return to the state. Then save the design.                                                                                                                   |

## [Adding a Bookmark](https://spdocs.synopsys.com/dow_retrieve/latest/training/dg/custom_compiler/CC_bookmarks.mp4)

You can add a bookmark to save the association between this viewport and this design context. You can add bookmarks to any open design.

## Loading Bookmarks

You can load bookmarks to make them available for use in this session. By default, bookmarks stored in the current working directory file bookmarks.xml loaded automatically on session start. The SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_LOCAL environment variable controls this operation.

To load bookmarks:

1. Begin by displaying the Bookmark Manager Tool. From the Console tab, choose Tools &gt; Bookmark Manager .
2. In the Bookmark Manager, choose File &gt; Load .

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

3. Browse to choose the correct XML file.
4. Click Open .
5. When you are done, choose File &gt; Close .

## Saving Bookmarks

You can save bookmarks to retain them for future sessions.

Use the Bookmark Manager to save bookmarks. To add a bookmark, see Adding a Bookmark.

To save bookmarks:

1. Begin by opening the Bookmark Manager Tool. From the Console tab, choose Tools &gt; Bookmark Manager .
2. In the Bookmark Manager, choose File &gt; Save As .
3. Enter a new file name, or browse to choose a bookmark XML file you want to overwrite.
4. Click Save .
5. When you are done, choose File &gt; Close .

## Deleting Bookmarks

You can delete bookmarks to remove them from use.

Use the Bookmark Manager to delete a bookmark.

## Constraint Manager Tool

Constraints are rules that designs must follow to ensure correct layout fabrication and operation. The constraints are either global or design-specific. Global constraints are defined in the technology database, but you can use the Constraint Manager to view and manage these constraints. You use the Constraint Editor to create and manage designspecific constraints.

This topic describes the following:

- Constraint Types and Sources
- About the Constraint Manager
- Displaying the Constraint Manager
- Adding and Deleting Process Constraint Parameters
- Grouping a Set of Process Constraints
- Specifying User-Defined Constraint Groups
- Enabling Alternate Foundry Constraints
- Constraint Manager Reference

## See Also

- Technology and Display Resource Files
- Constraint Editor Assistant

<!-- image -->

## Constraint Types and Sources

Different constraint types work together in the Custom Compiler environment to ensure correct-by-construction designs while providing some flexibility to accommodate special requirements.

The Custom Compiler environment interacts with the following constraint types:

| Constraint Type   | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | Source                      |
|-------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| Process           | A set of global rules and constraints that all designs must follow during layout and routing, such as spacing rules and clearance rules. For information about the rules and constraints in the technology database, see the Custom Compiler Technology and Display Resource File Reference Manual.               | Technology database         |
| Design-specific   | Constraints that the Layout Editor, Schematic Editor, and Custom Router must follow instead of or in addition to the process rules in the technology database. The design-specific constraints further restrict process constraints. You cannot set design-specific constraints that violate process constraints. | Constraint Editor Assistant |

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Figure 53 summarizes the concept of the different constraint sources and the input into the various Custom Compiler products.

Figure 53 Sources of Design Rules Used by Custom Compiler Tools

<!-- image -->

## About the Constraint Manager

Although process constraints are stored in the technology database, you can use the Constraint Manager to access the technology data.

The Constraint Manager is a graphical user interface that lets you:

- Display the process constraints and default design constraints.
- Create, edit, and delete default constraints in a design or technology database.
- Create and manage process constraint groups.
- Create and manage user-defined constraint groups.

For information about process constraints in the technology database, see the Custom Compiler Technology File and Display Resource Reference Manual .

2. Choose Tools &gt; Constraint Manager . The Constraint Manager opens.

| Toolbar           | Displays button commands. For more information, see Constraint Manager Toolbar.                                                                                                                                                   |
| Constraint Groups | Displays list of constraint groups. If you select a constraint group, the list of constraints that belong in the group appears in the Constraints pane. To group a set of constraints, see Grouping a Set of Process Constraints. |

## Adding Parameters

5. In the Type list, choose the data type.
6. In the Value box, type a value to assign to the new parameter.
7. On the toolbar, click Commit ( ).

The lists of associated constraints appear in the Constraint pane.

2. In the Constraints pane, select the constraint whose parameters you want to delete.
3. In the Parameters pane, select the parameter you want to delete. The row in the table is highlighted.

<!-- image -->

4. On the toolbar, click Delete ( ). A strikethrough mark appears over the parameter type and value. x

## Grouping a Set of Process Constraints

You can group a set of constraints within the design scope instead of having to add or update constraints within the technology scope. You can create constraint groups using one of the following:

- Technology file
- Constraint Manager

Regardless of the method you use, the constraint group you create is available for selection in the Constraint Group toolbar.

This section describes how to create constraint groups using the Constraint Manager. For instructions on how to create groups in the technology file, see the Custom Compiler™ Technology and Display Resource File Reference Manual . For information about the Constraint Group toolbar and constraint group selection, see Specifying User-Defined Constraint Groups.

To group a set of constraints:

1. Open the Constraint Manager . In the layout view of a design, choose Tools &gt; Constraint Manager .
2. Choose File &gt; New Group . Alternatively, on the Constraint Manager toolbar, click New Group ( ).

The Create Constraint Group dialog box opens.

<!-- image -->

## 3. Set the following options:

| Option   | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|----------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Database | (Optional) The database to associate with the constraint group. Choose one of the following: ◦ Design : The design in which the new constraint group is created. ◦ Tech: <lib_name> : The technology libraries associated with the active design. |
| Name     | The name of the new constraint group.                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Operator | The logical operator to apply to the constraint group. Choose one of the following: ◦ precedence : Uses the first found constraint. ◦ and : All hard constraints must be met. ◦ or : At least one of the hard constraints must be met.            |

4. When you are finished, click OK to save the changes and close the dialog box. The newly created group appears in the Constraint Manager.
5. To add constraints to the constraint group, Ctrl+drag a constraint from the Constraints list (a) to the newly created constraint group (b).

## Enabling Alternate Foundry Constraints

By default, foundry rules are applied when you work with designs in the Custom Compiler environment. However, you can specify alternate foundry constraints that replace existing foundry rules. For example, if the existing foundry constraint group consists of analog rules, you can enable a constraint group containing digital-specific rules.

This section describes the following:

- Workflow for Enabling Alternate Foundry Constraints
- Before You Start
- Defining Alternate Foundry Constraint Groups
- Applying the Alternate Foundry Rules in the Design
- Associating Track Region Definitions With Alternate Foundry Constraint Groups

## Workflow for Enabling Alternate Foundry Constraints

This topic presents the basic workflow for enabling alternate foundry constraints.

|   Step |                                                                       | See...                                                                                                                                                       |
|--------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|      1 | Review the requirements and considerations.                           | Before You Start                                                                                                                                             |
|      2 | Define the alternate foundry constraint group in the technology file. | One of the following methods: • Choosing the Constraint Group Using the Alternate Foundry Toolbar • Setting the leTechFoundryConstraintGroups Tcl Preference |
|      3 | Choose and apply the alternate foundry rules in the design.           | Applying the Alternate Foundry Rules in the Design                                                                                                           |

## Before You Start

Before setting up and using alternate foundry constraints, review the requirements and considerations to optimize the implementation.

The alternate foundry constraint groups must meet the following requirements and considerations:

- The alternate foundry constraint groups must contain a complete set of design rules.
- User-defined constraint groups have priority over alternate foundry constraint groups.
- Cut class, color, and wide-alignment rules must still be defined in the original foundry technology.
- You can specify the original foundry technology with the alternate constraint groups.
- You can specify incremental technology databases. Each technology within the technology graph can have its own alternate foundry constraint group.

<!-- image -->

## See Also

- Constraint Groups Section
- Grouping a Set of Process Constraints

## Defining Alternate Foundry Constraint Groups

You can define alternate rules for your designs instead of applying the default foundry constraints. Doing so lets you use the relevant rules for specific applications.

To designate a constraint group as an alternate foundry constraint group:

- In the Constraint Groups Section of the technology file, make sure the constraint group is defined with the -alternate true argument.

## See Also

- Grouping a Set of Process Constraints
- Workflow for Enabling Alternate Foundry Constraints
- Before You Start
- Applying the Alternate Foundry Rules in the Design

## Applying the Alternate Foundry Rules in the Design

While editing your design layout, you can choose the alternate foundry constraint group that is searched first in the Constraint Manager. This topic describes how to choose the alternate foundry constraint group.

This topic describes the two methods you can use to apply alternate foundry rules in the design:

- Choosing the Constraint Group Using the Alternate Foundry Toolbar
- Setting the leTechFoundryConstraintGroups Tcl Preference

## Choosing the Constraint Group Using the Alternate Foundry Toolbar

To choose the alternate foundry constraint group:

1. In the Layout Editor, choose Window &gt; Toolbars &gt; Alternate Foundry .

The Alternate Foundry toolbar appears.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

2. Choose the constraint group from the Alternate Foundry list.

## Setting the leTechFoundryConstraintGroups Tcl Preference

To set the leTechFoundryConstraintGroups Tcl preference:

- Type the following in the Custom Compiler Console:

db::setPrefValue leTechFoundryConstraintGroups -value "&lt;groupName&gt;"

## See Also

- Workflow for Enabling Alternate Foundry Constraints
- Before You Start
- Defining Alternate Foundry Constraint Groups

## Associating Track Region Definitions With Alternate Foundry Constraint Groups

In the Track Region Assistant, in addition to turning on or off the active state of individual tracks, you can associate track region definitions with the foundry or alternate foundry constraint groups.

In this case, when the design is opened and when the leTechFoundryConstraintGroups Tcl preference value changes, the active and visible states of the tracks are automatically set based on the foundry or alternate foundry in use.

<!-- image -->

To associate track region definitions with alternate foundry constraint groups:

- Define the foundryConstraintGroups attribute in the track region definitions that you want to associate with alternate foundry constraint groups. See trackDefs.

## See Also

- Setting Track Region Assistant Options

## Display Resource Editor Tool

This topic describes the following:

- About the Display Resource Data

## About the Display Resource Data

Display resources control how everything appears on the canvas in the design editors, such as the color of the canvas background, the colors of objects, the colors and styles of lines, and how colored objects are filled. Display resource data is stored in the display.tcl file. See Display Resource File.

## Note:

The Custom Compiler environment also supports third-party display resource data files in the DRF format ( display.drf ).

The Custom Compiler default display.tcl file is in the installation directory. If your company, project, or individual designers have different display preferences, you can optionally use overriding display.tcl files in the directories listed in Table 93. You can point to the directories using the corresponding environment variables. The startup process loads all of these files in the order shown. The last-loaded file overrides the previous file. For example, the specifications in the user-specific display.tcl file always overrides the settings in the project-specific display.tcl file.

Table 93 Locations of display.tcl Files

| Locations of display.tcl                                                                                   | Environment Variable      |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| Installation directory (auxx directory)                                                                    | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_INSTALL  |
| Directory for site-specific data (optional)                                                                | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_SITE     |
| Directory for project-specific data (optional)                                                             | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_PROJECT  |
| Directories for custom setup                                                                               | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_INITPATH |
| Directory for user-specific data                                                                           | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_USER     |
| User's home directory, where compatible third-party product files are stored                               | $HOME                     |
| Current working directory                                                                                  | $PWD                      |
| Directory for data that are saved when you exit the Custom Compiler tool and reloads them when you restart | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_LOCAL    |

If the $SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_USER environment variable is not defined, the startup process will search the $HOME/synopsys\_custom directory. If the $SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_LOCAL environment variable is not defined, the startup process will search the $PWD/synopsys\_custom directory. For details about setting up the environment variables, defining the startup sessions, and the different directories, see Defining Startup Settings.

If a directory contains a display.drf file and a display.tcl file, both will be loaded in the respective order. Because the .tcl file is loaded later, its content overrides the content in the .drf file.

You can modify the display resource data using one of the following methods:

- Using the Displaying the Display Resource Editor.
- Editing the display.tcl files. See the Display Resource Tcl chapter in the Custom Compiler Tcl Reference Manual .

## Displaying the Display Resource Editor

The Display Resource Editor is the interface you use to view and modify the data in the display.tcl files.

<!-- image -->

## To display the Display Resource Editor:

- From the Home tab or a design layout view, choose Tools &gt; Display Resource Editor .

To display the Display Resource Editor using the dr::showDisplayResourceEditor Tcl command, type the command in the Console tab or Console pane.

In the Display Resource Editor, you can select the layer-purpose pair (LPP) or the packet on the left. The associated display attributes appear on the right.

<!-- image -->

Examples of line styles are solid lines, dotted lines, and dashed lines. • Fill Style : Style used to fill an object or area. ## Managing Display Definitions

Because a single display definition might not be optimal for all designs, you can create different display definitions to accommodate the different designs. You can also create different display definitions to showcase different aspects of the same design.

This section describes the following:

- Creating Display Definitions
- Editing Display Attributes
- Renaming Display Definitions
- Deleting Display Definitions

## Creating Display Definitions

To create a display definition:

1. In the Display Resource Editor, choose Display &gt; New .
2. In the New Display dialog box:
- a. Type a unique Name for the new display definition.
- b. (Optional) Select Limit contents if you want to restrict the maximum number of Colors , Line Styles , and Stipples in the definition.
3. When you are finished, click Create . The name of the newly created display definition appears in the Display menu.
4. To display the newly created display definition, choose Display &gt; &lt;displayDefinitionName&gt;.
5. To edit the display attributes, see Editing Display Attributes.

<!-- image -->

## Editing Display Attributes

Each display definition consists of a list of LPPs, display Packets, and corresponding display attributes (line color, line style, fill style, and so on).

To edit a display attribute:

1. In the Display Resource Editor, select the LPP or Packet .

When a single packet or LPP is selected, the Packet: &lt;name&gt; is displayed. When nothing is selected, Packet Attributes is displayed. When multiple items are selected, Multiple Packets is displayed.

2. In the Packets area on the right side of the dialog box, choose different attribute values from the Fill Color , Outline Color , Stipple , Line Style , and Fill Style lists.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

If you want to add new or modify existing attribute values, click Edit , and then create or modify an attribute value. When you are finished, you should see the new or modified attribute value in the dialog box.

3. To reset any value to its previous state, click Reset .
4. To change the attributes of LPP/Packet, click Apply .

## Renaming Display Definitions

## Note:

All display definitions, except the default definition, are available for renaming.

To rename a display definition:

1. In the Display Resource Editor, choose the display definition you want to rename in the Display menu.
2. Choose Display &gt; Rename .
3. In the Rename Display dialog box, type a new name.
4. Click Rename . You should see the new name in the Display menu.

## Deleting Display Definitions

To delete a display definition:

1. In the Display Resource Editor, choose the display definition you want to delete in the Display menu.
2. Choose Display &gt; Delete.
3. In the Confirm Delete Display dialog box, click OK to proceed with the delete operation.

## Creating and Editing Display Packets and Packet Aliases

You can create display packets to define a set of attributes for association with a display definition. You can also create packet aliases to enable adjustment of display attributes without affecting their definitions in the technology file.

- Creating Packets
- Creating Packet Aliases
- Using Active Packet Aliases

## Creating Packets

You can create packets to define sets of visual attributes for design objects. Use the Display Resource Editor to create a packet.

To create a packet:

1. In the Display Resource Editor, click Packets .
2. (Optional) In the Packets list, choose a packet whose attributes are similar to the one you want to create.
3. Choose Edit &gt; New Packet .
4. Enter a packet name.
5. Edit attributes for this packet.

<!-- image -->

For any attribute you want to change, choose a predefined value from the menu.

To additionally alter the visual definition for this value, click Edit , make changes, and click OK .

6. When you are done, choose File &gt; Close .

<!-- image -->

## Creating Packet Aliases

You can create a packet alias to modify attributes for an existing packet without changing its packet definition in the technology file.

Use the Display Resource Editor to create a packet alias.

To create a packet alias:

1. In the Display Resource Editor, choose a packet.
2. Choose Edit &gt; New PacketAlias .
3. Enter a PacketAlias name.
4. When you are done, choose File &gt; Close .

## Using Active Packet Aliases

The active object is displayed using the active display packet alias. By default, this alias points to an active\_TrueColorBright display packet. This packet has no stipple, dashed line style, and color (RGB) 166 176 186. For a path, it appears as follows:

## Creating Colors, Stipples, and Line Styles

Create colors, stipples, and line styles to provide additional attributes for display packets to use.

## These sections cover:

- Creating Fill and Outline Colors
- Creating Stipple Patterns
- Creating Line Styles

## Creating Fill and Outline Colors

You can create a fill and outline colors by defining their display names, RGB (red, green, blue) luminosity values, and optionally, a blink setting.

Use the Display Resource Editor to create fill and outline colors.

To create fill or outline color:

1. In the Display Resource Editor, in the section for the Fill Color or Outline Color attribute, click Edit.
2. Click Add .
3. Enter a color name.
4. Adjust the RGB values by moving the cursor over the continuous tone bitmap, or choose by number.
5. To cause layers with this color to blink, click Blink .
6. Click OK .
7. When you are done, choose File &gt; Close .

## Creating Stipple Patterns

You can create a stipple pattern for fills by defining its display name, and a bitmap pattern, in pixels.

Use the Display Resource Editor to create stipple patterns.

<!-- image -->

To create a stipple pattern:

1. In the Display Resource Editor, in the section for the Stipple attribute, click Edit .
2. Click Add .

All displays support the built-in X stipple. This stipple is not defined as a bitmap, and it can be referenced in any packet definition. The X stipple causes an 'X' of fixed line width to be drawn from corner to corner in all rectangles, and rectangular polygons, leaving other shapes unfilled.

You can override the built-in X stipple in any display by creating a bitmap-based stipple named 'X' in that display.

3. Enter a stipple name.
4. Choose a base pattern size in number of pixels.
5. Use the cursor to select pixels for the base pattern.

To create a pattern with a dark background, define the fewer-pixel portion, and click Invert .

6. When you are done, choose File &gt; Close .

## Creating Line Styles

You can use the Display Resource Editor to create line styles. You might want different line styles to create visual distinctions between similar objects. For example, by default, the line styles for color n and color n Locked are different so that you can visually distinguish locked colors from unlocked colors on the canvas. With this visual aid, you do not need to use the Property Editor to check the color lock status.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

You can create a line style by defining its display name, a line width in pixels, and a onedimensional bit pattern (1s and 0s) of any length.

## To create a line style:

1. In the Display Resource Editor, in the section for the Line Style attribute, click Edit .
2. Click Add .
3. Enter a line style name.
4. Choose a pattern length, and a line width.
5. Use the cursor to select pixels for the pattern. (Optional) To create a pattern with a dark background, define the fewer-pixel portion, and click Invert .
6. When you are done, choose File &gt; Close .

## Managing Display Resources

The changes you make to the display definitions or display data is temporarily stored in memory. If you want to keep the changes for future use, you must save the changes.

## This section describes the following:

- Saving Display Resource Data
- Loading Display Resource Files

<!-- image -->

- Reloading Last-Saved Display Resource Files
- Reloading Default Display Resource Files
- Merging Display Resource Files

## Saving Display Resource Data

You can save modified display resource data from the current session to a display.tcl or display.drf file.

## Caution:

If you want Custom Compiler to automatically load the display resource data during startup, name the file display.tcl or display.drf and save it in one of the directories listed in About the Display Resource Data.

To save new or modified display resource data to a display file:

1. In the Display Resource Editor, choose File &gt; Save As . The Save Display Resource dialog box opens.
2. Select the location where you want to save the file.
3. Type the File name .
4. Choose a file type: Tcl or DRF.
5. (Optional) To save only the data that were modified in the current design session or since the last Reload operation, select Modifications Only .
6. Click Save .

## Loading Display Resource Files

During startup, Custom Compiler automatically loads the display.tcl or display.drf files as described in About the Display Resource Data. However, if you have a different display data file you want to use, you can load it using the Display Resource Editor.

To load a display resource file:

1. In the Display Resource Editor, choose File &gt; Load .
2. In the Load Display Resource File dialog box, locate and select the display.tcl or display.drf file.
3. Click Load .

## Reloading Last-Saved Display Resource Files

In case you want to revert to the last-saved or last-loaded display data, you can use the File &gt; Reload Display command. Doing so overwrites any modifications you made that you have not yet saved. If you want to keep the modifications, see Saving Display Resource Data.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

When you reload the last-saved display resource file, Custom Compiler loads the display.tcl files in the following directories, in the order shown:

| Locations of display.tcl                                                                          | Environment Variable      |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| Installation directory (auxx)                                                                     | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_INSTALL  |
| Directory for site-specific data                                                                  | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_SITE     |
| Directory for project-specific data                                                               | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_PROJECT  |
| Directories for custom setup                                                                      | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_INITPATH |
| Directory for user-specific data                                                                  | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_USER     |
| User's home directory, where compatible third-party product files are stored                      | $HOME                     |
| Current working directory                                                                         | $PWD                      |
| Directory for data that are saved when you exit Custom Compiler and reloads them when you restart | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_LOCAL    |

To reload the last-saved display resource data:

1. In the Display Resource Editor, choose File &gt; Reload Display . The Discard Display Resource Edits dialog box opens.
2. Click Overwrite to continue. The Resource Editor loads all the display.tcl or display.drf files in the order described in About the Display Resource Data.

## Reloading Default Display Resource Files

In case you want to revert to the original display data that were provided with the product, you can use the File &gt; Reload Default command. Doing so allows you to start from the original display setup.

When you reload the last-saved display resource file, Custom Compiler loads the display.tcl files in the following directories, in the order shown:

| Locations of display.tcl         | Environment Variable     |
|----------------------------------|--------------------------|
| Installation directory (auxx)    | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_INSTALL |
| Directory for site-specific data | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_SITE    |

<!-- image -->

| Locations of display.tcl                                                     | Environment Variable      |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| Directory for project-specific data                                          | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_PROJECT  |
| Directories for custom setup                                                 | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_INITPATH |
| Directory for user-specific data                                             | $SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_USER     |
| User's home directory, where compatible third-party product files are stored | $HOME                     |

To reload the original display resource files that were provided with the product:

1. In the Display Resource Editor, choose File &gt; Reload Default . The Discard Display Resource Edits dialog box opens.
2. Click Overwrite to continue. The Resource Editor loads all the original display.tcl or display.drf files in the order described in About the Display Resource Data.

## Merging Display Resource Files

You can combine the data from multiple display resource files into one display resource file. Note that when you list the files to merge, the file order determines the overriding sequence (the last file overrides all preceding files).

To merge display resource from multiple files:

1. In the Display Resource Editor, choose File &gt; Merge .
2. In the Merge Display Resource Files dialog box, click Add .

<!-- image -->

3. In the Select Source Files dialog box, locate and select the .tcl or .drf file, and then click Open .
4. Repeat step 3 to add additional files.
5. To change the order of the files, in the Merge Display Resource Files dialog box, select a file in the Source list and click Move Up or Move Down . Be aware that each file overrides the file that precedes it.
6. To remove a file from the list, select the file in the Source list and click Remove.
7. In the Destination area, click to select the location for the merged data file, type a File name , and click Save .
8. Choose the Format for the destination file ( TCL or DRF ). If you choose Auto , the format will be determined automatically, based on the filename extension you specified in step 7. If you did not specify a filename extension in step 7, the newly merged file will be in the TCL format by default.
9. (Optional) To prevent the data from being loaded into memory now, clear the Load Merged Data check box.
10. Click Merge .

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

| y0-9Flt                     | Static flight lines                                                                                                                                                       |
| y0-9Flt_dyn                 | Dynamic flight lines                                                                                                                                                      |

## Hierarchy Editor Tool

The Hierarchy Editor tool controls the number of instances edited at one time. Use this tool to design with hierarchy configurations.

This topic describes the following:

- Displaying the Hierarchy Editor
- Creating Hierarchy Configurations
- Editing Hierarchy Configurations
- Controlling Viewed Information
- Hierarchy Editor Menus
- Hierarchy Editor Toolbar

<!-- image -->

The Hierarchy Editor tool controls the number of instances edited at one time. Use this tool to design with hierarchy configurations.

This video tutorial shows how to use the Hierarchy Editor..

## [Displaying the Hierarchy Editor](https://spdocs.synopsys.com/dow_retrieve/latest/training/dg/custom_compiler/CC_hierarchy_editor.mp4)

You can create hierarchy configurations (config views) to work with a subset of selected instances in a design schematic. Hierarchy configurations limit the view depth. This controls the extent of the design the system evaluates in analysis operations. The Hierarchy Editor defines, manages, and maintains configuration views.

You use the Hierarchy Editor to work with hierarchy configuration (config) views.

<!-- image -->

The config cellview determines the switched master for each placed instance in a design. A switched master uses rules to control which instance view netlisters and other tools use in the design they process.

The config cellview also stores a reference to the root cellview of the hierarchy and all additional rules necessary to traverse (or bind) the design.

To open the Hierarchy Editor:

- Open the config view of a schematic and choose Tools &gt; Hierarchy Editor . The Hierarchy Editor opens in a new tab.

<!-- image -->

## Creating Hierarchy Configurations

Create hierarchy configurations by creating config cellviews. Through a config view, you can explore the design, set proper views for netlisters, and edit the design with concurrent visibility into the associated hierarchy.

Create config views from the source of your choice:

- Creating Configuration Views From an Existing Design
- Creating Configuration Views as New CellViews

## Creating Configuration Views From an Existing Design

Create a config view from an existing design to use this library, cell, and view combination as the switched master.

1. Begin by opening the Hierarchy Editor. Open the config view of a schematic, and choose Tools &gt; Hierarchy Editor .
2. Open the Hierarchy Editor: Choose Tools &gt; Hierarchy Editor .
3. Confirm the Top Cellview or choose a new design.
4. (Optional) If you did not supply a template, define the View Search List by entering view names.

A view search list is an ordered list of view names that determines the switched master. You can set the default using the heEditorDefaultViewSearchList preference.

The views found are governed by the search list rules you are defining. If a cell does not contain any of the views listed in the view search list and view selection is not set, the view found is listed as unbound in red text.

After the View Search List is added, the configuration for the top cellview is created.

To view the hierarchy, and see the view found for each instance, expand the root of the tree.

5. (Optional) For an explanation of the rule governing a view found, select an instance in the tree and choose Edit &gt; Explain (or right-click the instance and choose Explain ). (See Explaining Found Hierarchy Views).
6. (Optional) If you did not supply a template, define a View Stop List by entering names of views to define the lowest descent level for that leaf. You can set the default using the heEditorDefaultViewStopList preference.

Alternatively, allow the tool to determine stop levels where it encounters views holding no instances.

7. (Optional) You can change the view to which an instance is bound by clicking in the Selected field and selecting from the drop-down menu. You can select multiple instances to change at one time. (See Selecting and Clearing Scoped Views).

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

When you modify the view rule in the drop-down menu,

- The occurrence of the scoped view is cleared, and the instance scoped view is set.
- A reminder message appears:
- Instance scoped view changes to 'ABC' and the occurrence of the scoped view is cleared
- The occurrence of the instance scoped view is cleared
8. (Optional) You can change the view to which an occurrence is bound by clicking in the Selected field and selecting from the drop-down menu. Selecting a view adds an occurrence rule to the configuration associated with the design editor.
9. (Optional) To bind the instance (or multiple instances, if selected) or occurrence to an external netlist, choose &lt;Bind to Netlist Text&gt; to open the Select External Netlist File to Bind dialog box. Select a File Name , View Name , and Language .

<!-- image -->

Check Overwrite to overwrite the cellView, otherwise a warning is issued and the Hierarchy Editor does not overwrite the view or set the binding.

(SPICE/CDL only) Check Create Virtual Terminals to enable the options for creating certain terminals in the subcircuit declaration as virtual. See Table 30 in the topic Importing Design Netlist Data as Text Views for details on these options.

Click OK to close the dialog box.

10. (Optional) To bind the instance (or multiple instances, if selected) or occurrence to an external netlist file without importing to the OA database, choose &lt;Bind to Netlist File&gt; to open the Select External Netlist File to Bind dialog box. Select a File Name and Language .

## Note:

When you select &lt;Bind to Netlist File&gt; , the path last browsed becomes the default path. Set the heExternalNetlistFileBrowsePath preference to use this default path.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

As seen in the preceding example, you can use environment variables in the netlist file path; the tool automatically lists available environment variables. When selecting netlist files, the tool automatically detects the netlist format from the file name extension.

Click OK to close the dialog box.

11. Choose File &gt; Save .

## Creating Configuration Views as New CellViews

Create a config view from a new cellView to define the switched master as you create the cellView.

1. Open the Library Manager: Tools &gt; Library Manager .
2. Create the cellView: File &gt; New &gt; CellView .
3. Select the library, cell, and the Hierarchy Editor.
4. Choose the view name config or enter a different name.
5. Click OK .

The hierarchy is populated from the root cellview. (After you open the Hierarchy Editor, and define the view search and view stop lists, the hierarchy expands to display the tree corresponding to the top level of the design).

6. Save the current Configuration cellView: File &gt; Save (Needed) .

7. Save the unchanged Configuration cellView: File &gt; Save .

## Note:

The Save icon displays an asterisk on the upper-right corner when there are unsaved changes.

Edit hierarchy configuration by working with config views.

## Undoing and Redoing Configuration View Modifications

Undo or redo config modifications to reverse or reactivate changes. (To reverse or reactivate general session operations, use the Transaction History Assistant).

Begin by opening the Hierarchy Editor. Open the config view of a schematic, and choose Tools &gt; Hierarchy Editor .

- To undo the last config modification, in the Hierarchy Editor choose Edit &gt; Undo or click the button in the toolbar. In the toolbar, you can select from a list of recent modifications by clicking the Down Arrow.
- To redo the last config modification, in the Hierarchy Editor choose Edit &gt; Redo or click the button in the toolbar. In the toolbar, you can select from a list of recent modifications by clicking the Down Arrow.

## Explaining Found Hierarchy Views

Explain found views to learn the rule that determines how a view is found for this configuration.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

1. Begin by opening the Hierarchy Editor. Open the config view of a schematic, and choose Tools &gt; Hierarchy Editor .
2. To explain the view found for a cellview or instance, position the cursor in the Bound column, right-click the mouse, and choose Explain from the menu.

Alternatively, you can select the cell or instance first, and then choose Edit &gt; Explain .

<!-- image -->

## Importing Attributes From Existing Configuration Views

Import attributes from existing config views to easily supply them to a current config view. You can import the top library/cell/view combination, stop lists, global view search lists, open view lists, view name groups, and selection rules.

1. Begin by opening the Hierarchy Editor. Open the config view of a schematic, and choose Tools &gt; Hierarchy Editor .
2. In the Hierarchy Editor, choose Edit &gt; Import .
3. Specify the source config cellview.
4. Check mark the attributes to import.
5. Click Import .

## Specifying a Template for a Hierarchy Configuration View

Specify a template for a config view to set the view search and view stop list for the current configuration from predefined settings associated with a tool.

1. Begin by opening the Hierarchy Editor. Open the config view of a schematic, and choose Tools &gt; Hierarchy Editor .
2. In the Hierarchy Editor, choose Edit &gt; Use Template , and select a simulator by name.

<!-- image -->

3. (Optional) Supply a template by choosing Edit &gt; Use Template , and selecting a tool

name, or by clicking the Use Template

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Templates are available for AMS, AMSBehavioral, AMSText, CSM, HSPICE, Spectre, SpectreAMS, SpectreAMSBehavioral, VHDL, and Verilog. Supplying a template populates the design cell list and view search and stop lists.

## Using Hierarchy View Name Groups

View Name Groups define aliases for commonly used lists of View Names. For example, you can group the view name list VERILOG VLG VLG2 VHDL into a group named DIGHDL. View name groups are referenced by prepending a percent character ('%') before the View Name Group.

You can add, edit, (or delete) view name groups to change view name groups associated with a config view.

To use hierarchy view name groups:

1. Begin by opening the Hierarchy Editor. Open the config view of a schematic, and choose Tools &gt; Hierarchy Editor .
2. In the Hierarchy Editor, choose Edit &gt; View Name Groups .
3. Choose an option:

To add a new group, in the dialog box add an empty row (if necessary) by right-clicking the mouse, and choosing Add from the menu. In the group name column, enter the name of the group. In the view list column, specify the view search list.

To edit a name or view list, select the corresponding field, and edit.

To delete a name group, select the row, and choose Delete .

button.

The system validates all changes and, for invalid edits, reports errors.

4. Click OK .

2. In the Hierarchy Editor, choose Edit &gt; Options .

## Searching Configuration Views

You can search in config views by instance name, library name, and cell name.

To search a config view:

1. Press Ctrl+F or choose View &gt; Find . The Find window appears at the bottom of the Hierarchy Editor.
2. Enter a search term in the Find window. Press Enter, or use the Next and Previous buttons to scroll through the found items.
3. To close the Find window, click .

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Filtering Configuration Views on Libraries or Cells

You can hide selected libraries and cells from the configuration view.

To filter a configuration view:

1. Click . The Filter dialog box appears.
2. Select the Library (and Cell , if required) on which to filter.
3. Click to add a filter row under the current row, or to delete a filter row.
4. Click OK to apply the filter(s) and close the dialog box.

## Synchronizing Design and Hierarchy Data

Synchronize data by refreshing the design on demand or automatically, or by refreshing the config view automatically.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Begin by opening the Hierarchy Editor. Open the config view of a schematic, and choose Tools &gt; Hierarchy Editor .

- To synchronize the config view with the design on demand, choose View &gt; Refresh in the Hierarchy Editor.
- To update the visible tree or cell hierarchy after each design change, choose View &gt; Auto Refresh Design in the Hierarchy Editor.
- To update the visible tree or cell hierarchy after each config change, choose View &gt; Auto Refresh Config in the Hierarchy Editor.

## Enabling Automatic Cross Selection Between Hierarchy Editor and Design Editor

1. Begin by opening the Hierarchy Editor. Open the config view of a schematic, and choose Tools &gt; Hierarchy Editor .
2. To enable automatic cross selection between Hierarchy Editor and Design Editor, choose View &gt; Auto Cross Select in the Hierarchy Editor.
3. Show, and adjust the top cellview displayed, by choosing View &gt; Top Cell View .

<!-- image -->

4. Right-click on any instance to choose:
- Fit : Zooms to the selected instance or instances in the latest opened window with the same configuration.
- Select in Design : Selects the selected instance or instances in the latest opened window with the same configuration.
- Deselect in Design : Deselects the selected instance or instances in the latest opened window with the same configuration.

<!-- image -->

## Showing Hierarchy View Search and Stop Lists

Show hierarchy search and stop lists in the Hierarchy Editor.

1. Begin by opening the Hierarchy Editor. Open the config view of a schematic, and choose Tools &gt; Hierarchy Editor .
2. Specify the information to show.
- Show, and adjust the top cellview displayed, by choosing View &gt; Top Cell View .
- Show the search and stop lists by choosing View &gt; Global View Search List , and View &gt; Global View Stop List .
- Show the library search list (useful for schematic driven layout design) by choosing View &gt; Global Library Search List .

## Showing Hierarchy Tree or Cell Views

In the Hierarchy Editor, you can show the tree or cell view of a design.

<!-- image -->

To show the tree or cell view:

1. Begin by opening the Hierarchy Editor. Open the config view of a schematic, and choose Tools &gt; Hierarchy Editor .
2. In the Hierarchy Editor, choose a view:
- Choose View &gt; Tree (or click Tree ) to list the complete hierarchical instance tree. Instance rules apply here.
- Choose View &gt; Cell (or click Cell ) to list each cellview in the design. Cell-based rules apply here. The cell-based hierarchy view lets you bind all instances of a selected cell.

The tree view is the default view. You can set the cell view as the default using the following Tcl command:

db::setPrefValue heViewType -value cell

3. Expand or collapse the hierarchy by right-clicking in the Instance column and choosing Expand All or Collapse All . (Select more than one instance row to expand or collapse all selected instances).

<!-- image -->

## Showing and Hiding Vector Bits

From the Show Vector Bits dialog box, you can expand vector bits by input bit range.

<!-- image -->

Select the display bits from the list or input the display range by updating the text field. The default display range value is the full vector range of this vector instance.

Choose OK to show the vector bits on the same level as the vector instance. These items are in gray text. The bits range number shows on the vector instance item if the display range is not the full bit range of this vector. After Show Vector Bits , this vector item is not allowed to expand, and the arrow icon is hidden.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

When a vector shows bits on the list, Hide Vector Bits is enabled, and you can hide the implicit bits without any rule in the list. If a bit contains any rule, it cannot be hidden.

## Selecting the View or Library

You can select either the View Selection or the Library Selection dialog boxes to select the following lists:

- View search list
- View stop list
- Library search list

In the Library Selection dialog box, the opened libraries and keyword, %PLACED are listed in the Available Library . When you choose a library and click , the selected library is moved to the Selected Library list. The order of the available and selected library lists can be reordered by dragging and dropping the files. The library search list is filled according to the order of the selected library list, and you can filter the case-sensitive libraries. D

<!-- image -->

The View Selection dialog box shows only commonly used views in the Available View list. Therefore, you can add views by typing them in the provided field, and separating them by space. If the views you add are set to the view search or stop list, they are added to the heEditorAvailableViewList preference, which is loaded the next time you launch the dialog box. You can remove a view from the available view list by clicking x beside the view. The preference is then updated. However, if the view remains in VSL or VTL, the preferences are not be updated.

<!-- image -->

## Viewing Unbound Cell or Instance Information

If there are unbound cells or instances in the config view, the Show Unbound

<!-- image -->

Information button is enabled in the toolbar. (If the button is not enabled, there are no unbound cells or instances in this config view).

<!-- image -->

The Show Unbound Information button is available when:

- You are opening the config view for the first time.
- You have just refreshed the view (using View &gt; Refresh ).
- You have just switched from the tree view to the cell view.

<!-- image -->

To view unbound cell or instance information:

<!-- image -->

1. Select a cell (in the cell view) or instance (in the tree view) and click the Show Unbound Information button.

<!-- image -->

The Unbound Information dialog box appears.

<!-- image -->

2. (Optional) Click Export to save the unbound information to a text file.
3. Click OK to exit the dialog box.

<!-- image -->

## Selecting and Clearing Scoped Views

To change the scoped view selection rule for instances or cells:

1. In either a tree or cell view, select an instance or a cell (or multiple instances/cells) and right-click in the Selected column.
2. Choose the required view from the menu that appears to set the selection rule.

The configuration view and the design are automatically updated because the Auto Refresh Design and Auto Refresh Config options under the View menu are enabled by default.

3. Remove the scoped view selection rule (for cells or instances) by selecting an instance or a cell and right-clicking in the Selected column and choosing Clear Cell Scoped View Selection or Clear Instance Scoped View Selection from the menu. (You can select multiple instances/cells on which to perform this operation).

<!-- image -->

## About the Library Manager

Every design in the Custom Compiler environment has the following components:

| Design Component   | Description                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Library            | The collection of data that comprise a whole or partial design that you create. Common data, or reference libraries, contain master copies of cells that you can reference in multiple designs. |
| Cell               | Building blocks of the designs.                                                                                                                                                                 |
| View               | Representations of a cell. For example, a cell can have a schematic view, a layout view, or a symbol view.                                                                                      |

The Library Manager displays information about the designs and lets you manage libraries, cells, and views for the design process.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## For example:

- The Libraries pane uses icons to distinguish between library sources. Library names without icons are Custom Compiler libraries. Fusion Compiler, IC Compiler II, and IC Compiler libraries have the following icon associations:

<!-- image -->

Fusion Compiler

<!-- image -->

IC Compiler II library

<!-- image -->

IC Compiler library

The list of libraries and the category of libraries displayed in the Library Manager are defined in the library definitions ( lib.defs ) file. The file maps the libraries to their physical locations on the computer disk. You can view and edit the files using the Library Definitions Editor. See Editing Library Definitions and Creating Library Categories.

- You can use the Cell Categories pane to simplify and organize large lists of cells.
- When you choose a library, cell, or view, the Preview pane shows the directory corresponding to your selection or a thumbnail view of the cellview, the date and time it was last modified, the user who last modified the cellview, the owner of the directory, and the read/write permissions.

By default, the Preview pane appears under the Views pane. To move it so that is beneath all the other panes, choose View &gt; Display Preview Horizontally or set the dmPreviewPosition Tcl preference to bottom .

- When you choose the library, cell, and view, a thumbnail of the design displays in the Preview pane to provide visual confirmation.

To update preview, choose Edit &gt; Update Preview , or right-click a library, cell, or cellview and select Update Preview . The corresponding Tcl command is dm::updatePreviews .

- The Views pane uses the icon to distinguish between designs created in the Custom Compiler environment and in third-party products. (For the icon to display, you must set the dmMarkSavedDesigns Tcl preference to true ).
- Colored cell and view names indicate that they are already open and are in either the edit mode (purple) or read-only mode (green).

By default, the Views pane is displayed. If you prefer to display a customized pane instead, you can hide the View pane. To hide the Views pane, set the dmHideViews Tcl preference to true . To create a customized pane, see Tools for Designing.

## Displaying the Library Manager

The Library Manager lets you view and manage libraries. You can open multiple Library Manager windows, as needed.

To display the Library Manager, use one of these methods:

- From the Console tab or any open design window, choose Tools &gt; Library Manager .
- In any design window toolbar, click the Library Manager button.

The Library Manager consists of the following:

<!-- image -->

| Component   | Description                                                                  |
|-------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Menu Bar    | Contains menus of commands. For more information, see Library Manager Menus. |
| Toolbar     | Displays button commands. For more information, see Library Manager Toolbar. |

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

| Component                           | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Filter Boxes                        | Filters the list directly below the text box to find the closest match. You can use wildcards (*) or partial text. When you provide a partial word, the filter lists all the names that contain the partial word. Cell Categories , Cells , and Views cannot be filtered if no library is selected or if multiple libraries are selected. |
| List of Libraries, Cells, and Views | Library , Cell Categories , Cells, and Views display a hierarchical list of items that can be filtered by the filter boxes.                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

The Library Manager appears and displays the list of libraries. The Library Manager also lists read-only libraries. If you select a read-only library in the Library list:

<!-- image -->

- Open Read-Only in the upper right corner of the window is disabled.
- The design you select in the read-only library opens as read-only.
- Some File and Edit commands are disabled.
- The Edit &gt; Move dialog box does not let you select read-only libraries as the source.
- The Edit &gt; Copy dialog box does not let you select read-only libraries as the destination.
- User-interface operations, such as drag-and-drop actions, are disabled.

You can optionally open a second Library Manager window by clicking New Library Manager at the top of the first Library Manager window.

You can pin the Library Manager using the context menu item Pin Library Manager , available by right-clicking on the Library Manager tab.

## Showing and Hiding Libraries and Cells

You can show and hide libraries and cells in the Library Manager. Hiding libraries and cells can be useful if the PDK contains too many libraries and cells, and you only want to display those that are used in your design.

This topic describes the following:

- Before You Start
- Showing and Hiding Libraries
- Showing and Hiding Cells

## Before You Start

To show or hide the top-level library, you must have permission to modify the lib.defs file. To show or hide library cells, you must have write access to *.Cats files and their directories.

The shown attribute of the dmCell object works independently of the show and hide procedures in the Library Manager. For example, if you want to show a cell but the shown attribute is false, you must change it to true in addition to using the show procedure in the Library Manager as described in this topic.

## Creating New Libraries

You can create a new library to define a logical collection of data representing a complete design or some portion of it. Additionally, you can create libraries to define common data shared among several designs. A library is the top organizational level of design data.

To create a new library:

1. In the Library Manager:
- Select any location in the Libraries list, right-click the mouse, and choose New .
- From the File menu, choose New &gt; Library .
- From the Toolbar , click Create Library .

The New Library dialog box opens.

<!-- image -->

2. Type the library Name .
3. Browse to choose a Directory to hold the library.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The system stores this directory in the current library definition file. The stored path includes both the parent directory you entered and the library directory.

## 4. Select the library Type :

- OpenAccess (FileSys) (Default)
- 3DIC Compiler
- Fusion Compiler
- ICC2
- ICC

## 5. Set the options for the OpenAccess library.

For the description of Fusion Compiler options, see Preparing Design Libraries for Fusion Compiler co-designing. For the description of ICC2 options, see Preparing Design Libraries for IC Compiler II co-designing. For the description of ICC options, see Preparing Libraries for IC Compiler Co-Designing.

| Settings                 | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|--------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Technology               | None creates a new library using the process-neutral technology file supplied with the environment. Import File uses the technology file you import by browsing to choose it. Attach uses the technology from the library you select from the list box. Reference uses an ordered list of open libraries to be incrementally referenced from the technology of the new library. Alternatively, the browse button invokes the Technology References dialog box, which lists all the currently open libraries with technology databases. |
| Enable Pcell Caching     | Specifies a PCell cache to be used for supermasters in the library, and adds an ASSIGN statement to the library definition file with the cache directory location.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Enable Parameter Overlay | Specifies that component description format parameters can be overlaid, and adds an ASSIGN statement to the library definition file with the component description format file location.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

<!-- image -->

| Settings           | Description                                                                                                                                                                |
|--------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Enable Compression | Select a value from the drop-down list to compress a new library. If the dmEnableLibraryCompression preference is set to true , the new library is compressed on creation. |

6. Click OK .

In the Library Definition editor, you can show either the absolute path or relative path to the lib.defs location. Use the Use Absolute Paths option in the Edit menu of the Library Definition window.

You can also set the path using the dmLibDefEditorUseAbsolutePaths preference. If true , displays absolute path. If false , displays relative path. Default: false .
