## Creating a Split

The tool picks a set of independent DTCO parameters whose values are changed from current nominal values. Only independent DTCO parameters are candidates for participating in a Split.

After specifying a set of updated values for DTCO parameters, you can specify a new target library from a process Create Split which is created by clicking the Run button. This creates a copy of all cells that designs in the source library with the target library name and remaster instances to come from the target library. All cells in the source library (even if they are in other libraries) are copied to the target library.

<!-- image -->

To create a split from DTCO parameters:

1. Specify the source library to be copied in the Source Library selection field.
2. Specify the target library name in the Target Library Name text field. It is important to name the Target Library with indicative name which tells about DTCO parameters that have been changed in the corresponding split.
3. Click the Browse button in the Target Library Directory text field to specify the target library directory from the Select Target Library Directory dialog box.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

4. (Optional) View names specified in the Exclude Views text field are not copied during a split operation.
5. Using Click to Add to add new row in the DTCO parameter table.
6. Add DTCO parameters by clicking the arrow from each row in the DTCO parameter table.

<!-- image -->

The table contains the following columns and toolbar:

<!-- image -->

| Option   | Description                                                                                             |
|----------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Name     | Selects one or more independent DTCO parameters from the source library by clicking the arrow.          |
| Value    | Displays the values of parameters when the parameters are specified. New values can be added or edited. |

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

| Option           | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| ReRun DTCO Steps | Based on the modified parameters, this column reruns steps affected by the changes to the DTCO parameter. This information relies on the Category attribute of the DTCO parameter with the correct values. |
|                  | Deletes the selected row.                                                                                                                                                                                  |

7. If the split involves changes to the setups to the TCAD process simulations that are not exposed as DTCO parameters, then specifies the information to be updated for Parasitic Extraction , Transistor Modeling , and Interconnect Characterization in the Setup section. The values entered for various files are stored in the corresponding source library and the corresponding xml file (libraryName/tcad\_prefs.xml).
8. (Optional) The Post Callback Procedure Name is provided to execute a callback after completing Create Split process. The callback procedure has a signature of source library name, target library name and list of DTCO parameters with name, old value, and new value for each parameter that was specified into the Create Split dialog box.
9. Click Run to split to a new library which copied all cells from the source library.

<!-- image -->

## Design Reviews

The Custom Compiler design review system allows you to review design schematics and layouts, provide feedback, respond to feedback, and track review status. The built-in system enables collaborations between design and layout teams.

This chapter contains the following topics:

- About the Design Review System
- Workflows for Design Reviews
- Setting Up Design Review Policies
- Setting Up Automatic Review Notifications
- Creating, Editing, and Managing Design Reviews
- Opening an Existing Review
- Exporting Reviews
- Review Assistant Reference

## About the Design Review System

The Custom Compiler design review system consists of the Review Assistant and the Review Manager. The Review Assistant lets you enter and respond to feedback. The Review Manager lets you browse the design libraries and locate existing reviews of interest.

This topic describes the following:

- Review Assistant
- Review Manager
- Review Data Structure

<!-- image -->

- Review Database
- Review Process

## Review Assistant

The Review Assistant is the graphical user interface that lets you create and edit reviews.

You use the Review assistant to:

- Start, end, or delete reviews while in the Schematic Editor, Symbolic Editor, or Layout Editor.
- Enter review feedback without editing the design. The feedback can consist of text, annotations, and marked screen captures.
- Respond to the review feedback.
- Modify and track the status of the review feedback.

The Review Assistant supports entering and viewing comments in languages, including Chinese, Korean, and Japanese. To enable this support, start the ibus-setup executable on your computer and follow the instructions.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Review comments created on different hierarchy levels of the design can all be accessed from the Review Assistant.

<!-- image -->

- The Review Assistant displays the hierarchy levels up to the Stop Level .
- To facilitate design reviews, the review comments in the assistant are synchronized with the annotations in the design. When reviewing layouts, double-clicking the level\_n review item in the assistant descends in place. When reviewing schematics, doubleclicking the level \_n review item descends to level\_n.

In the schematic example shown, double-cilcking the Level 2 annotation in the assistant descends to design level 2 and displays the annotations on the canvas.

- If reviews on different hierarchy levels have the same name, the assistant displays the review name and merges the annotations from both levels.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Review Manager

The Review Manager is the graphical user interface that lets you search for reviews of interest.

You use the Review Manager to:

- Search for review of interest among design libraries. Available filters let you narrow the search.
- Browse the list of existing reviews for selected designs.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Review Data Structure

The Custom Compiler design review consists of reviews, issues, and annotations. Understanding the structure helps you determine how you set up the review policies and how to organize the reviews.

In the Custom Compiler environment, a design can have multiple reviews. Each review has a description, an associated severity, and multiple issues.

An issue can consist of a set of annotations or an image. When you create an issue, the canvas state and the set of annotations or images are preserved.

<!-- image -->

All review items are stored in a review database and are accessed using the Review Assistant.

<!-- image -->

## Review Database

The design review data is stored in a review database that is closely associated with the corresponding design. Understand the review database and its relationship with the design can help you quickly navigate and locate reviews of interest.

The review database stores a set of reviews for a given cellview (schematic, symbol, or layout), and is automatically generated when you initiate a review for the cellview. The review database is also a cellview with a hierarchical OpenAccess (OA) database for storage. The review cellview exists in the same oaCell as the cellview that is reviewed.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

For easy identification of the review cellview, it has the same name as the reviewed cellview with an appended suffix (Tcl preference: dcReviewCellViewSuffix ). The default suffix is .review . For example, the review cellview for lib1/cell1/layout is lib1/cell1/ layout.review .

## Review Process

The Custom Compiler design review process is based on the Review Data Structure.

The following figure shows a simplified design review process that uses the Review Assistant. A reviewer initiates the review process (opens the review database for write operations), creates one or more review items, and adds one or more issues (each with annotations and screen shots) for each review item. See Review Data Structure.

The reviewer then ends the review process, that is, saves and changes the review database to a read mode.

<!-- image -->

The review assignee then views the review items and examines each issue. The assignee can add comments to each review item and issue, and view the already existing comments. Each review item can then be marked approved, waived, fixed, or closed to conclude the specific review item.

## See Also

- Workflows for Design Reviews

## Workflows for Design Reviews

The design review process consists of two main tasks: setting up and maintaining reviews, and conducting reviews.

This topic provides the following:

- Workflow for Setting Up Design Reviews
- Workflow for Conducting Reviews

## Workflow for Setting Up Design Reviews

Before design reviews can be started, administrators should set up design review policies to define review users and permissions. In addition, if you can optionally set up automatic email notification so that members and approvers are aware of new or modified reviews.

The following table shows the workflow steps for setting up the design reviews.

|   Step |                                                        | See...                                    |
|--------|--------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
|      1 | Set up the design review policy for your organization. | Setting Up Design Review Policies         |
|      2 | (Optional) Set up automatic review notifications.      | Setting Up Automatic Review Notifications |

## Setting Up Design Review Policies

Design review policies enforce rules implemented by your organization. The policies define users and their permission levels for various design review activities.

This topic describes the following:

- About Design Review Policies
- Default Design Review Policy
- Creating Design Review Policies
- Modify Existing Design Review Policies

## About Design Review Policies

A design review policy defines review users and review permissions as follows:

| Policy Component   | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Users              | Review users can be one of the following: • Creator: Creates the review. • Assignee: Is assigned an issue. • Member: Is a participant in the review. • Approver: Approves the proposed modifications.                                                                                                             |
| Permissions        | Review users can have permission to: • Create issues, add review annotations in the design, and add images in the review comments. • Modify issues, review annotations in the design, and images in the review description. • Delete issues, review annotations in the design, and images in the review comments. |

## Default Design Review Policy

A default design review policy is provided, but it is not activated. The policy is defined as follows:

| Operation   | Description                                                                                                 |
|-------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Create      | Review users can create issues, add review annotations in the design, or add images in the review comments. |
| Modify      | Review users can modify issues, review annotations in the design, or images in the review comments.         |

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

| Operation   | Description                                                                                                         |
|-------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Delete      | Review users can delete reviews or issues within a review. Review users cannot delete review annotations or images. |

To activate the default design review policy, run the dc::setPolicy Tcl command as follows:

dc::setPolicy default

## Creating Design Review Policies

You can create your own design review policies for your organization. To create a new set of design review policies, use the dc::addPolicy Tcl command.

## Modify Existing Design Review Policies

To modify an existing design review policy, use the dc::addPolicy Tcl command to overwrite the existing policy. For example, to modify the default design review policy, you can use the dc::addPolicy command as follows:

```
dc::addPolicy default -canCreateProc newCanCreate -canDeleteProc newCanDelete -canModifyProc newCanModify
```

## Setting Up Automatic Review Notifications

Design review members and approvers can be notified of any new or modified review input. This topic describes how to set up automatic notifications.

To set up the automatic review notification:

1. Create a Tcl procedure for sending email notifications.

In the Tcl procedure:

- Use the sendmail Linux command, or an equivalent method for email transfers.
- Include to , subject , and body variables.

## Examples:

```
proc sendmail {to subject body} proc custom_notification {to subject body}
```

<!-- image -->

2. Set the dcReviewNotificationProc Tcl preference to specify the procedure you created in step 1.

For example:

```
db::setPrefValue dcReviewNotificationProc -value send_email_proc
```

3. When you create reviews, make sure you define the Approver(s) and Member(s) in the Create Review dialog box.

Only the defined approvers and members receive email notifications. Email notifications are automatically sent when you end reviews.

## Starting Design Review Sessions

Starting design reviews in the Review Assistant enables functions that permit you to add and edit reviews and issues.

To start a design review:

- On the Review Assistant toolbar, click Start Review .

<!-- image -->

As soon as you start a review, a review cellview (.review) is automatically generated.

## Creating New Reviews

To create a review for a design:

1. On the Review Assistant toolbar, click New Review .

<!-- image -->

The Create Review dialog box opens.

<!-- image -->

2. In the Description box:
- a. Type the review title on the first line. The title appears in the Title column in the Review Assistant.
- b. Type a description for the review on subsequent lines. The description appears in the Description section of the Review Assistant.

<!-- image -->

3. Choose the Severity of the review comments:
4. Specify the Assignee , the recipient of the review.
5. Specify the list of review Approver(s) , users who can set the review as Approved , Closed , or Waived .
4. Type the space-separated list of user names in the Approver(s) box. Alternatively, click , and select the user names.

| Argument    | Description                                      |
|-------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| Enhancement | New features to be added to the existing design. |
| Critical    | Defects that must be fixed.                      |
| Information | Notes to the designers or team.                  |

<!-- image -->

You must define approvers if you want approvers and review members to automatically receive notifications when you add or modify reviews.

6. Specify the review Member(s) , users who are notified of the review but are not required to approve.

<!-- image -->

Type the space-separated list of user names in the Member(s) box. Alternatively, click , and select the user names.

You must define members if you want approvers and review members to automatically receive notifications when you add or modify reviews.

## Copying Reviews

After you add a design review, you can copy the same review.

<!-- image -->

## To copy a review:

1. In the Review Assistant, select the review, and click Copy Review .
2. To add one or more library, cell, views to for review, click Add in the Destination section. The Add View dialog box opens.
3. Enter the Library, Cell, View and click OK or Apply .

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The library, cell, view appears in the Destination section in the Copy Review dialog box.

4. (Optional) To delete a destination from a library, cell, view from the Destination section, select the library, cell, view and click Remove .
5. The description of the copied design review appears in the Description box. You can edit the description, if needed.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

6. Select the Include Issues box to copy the design review annotations associated with the review. By default, this box is not selected.
7. Click OK or Apply. The copied review appears in the Review Assistant table.

## Editing Reviews

After you add a review, you can edit it to set the review status or change the original review information, such as the title, description, assignee, or approvers.

To edit a review:

1. In the Review Assistant, select the review, and click Edit Review .

<!-- image -->

The Edit Review dialog box opens.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

2. Choose the review Status to indicate the current state of the selected review:
3. Set or modify the remaining options as described in Creating New Reviews.

| Argument   | Description                                                |
|------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| Open       | The review is in progress.                                 |
| Approved   | The review is finished and all issues have been addressed. |
| Fixed      | The review issues have been fixed.                         |
| Waived     | The review is no longer applicable or under consideration. |
| Closed     | Reviewers should no longer view or add issues or comments. |

## Adding Annotations in a Review

You can add annotations in the design to let designers know the locations of issues. Annotations include text callouts, arrows, ellipses, and so on. The annotations are overlays and do not alter the original design.

When you add review annotations, you are creating issues that are stored as part of the review in the Review Assistant. Each issue can contain multiple annotations. Keep this organization in mind when you create review annotations.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

To add annotations in a review:

1. In the Review Assistant, select the review.
2. On the Review Assistant toolbar, click Add Annotation .

<!-- image -->

The Add Review Annotation dialog box opens.

<!-- image -->

3. In the Description box:
- a. Type the issue title on the first line. The title appears in the Title column in the Review Assistant.
- b. Type a description for the issue on subsequent lines. The description appears in the Description section of the Review Assistant.
4. Select the Type of annotation you want to add.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

| Argument          | Description   |
|-------------------|---------------|
| Callout Object    |               |
| Callout Highlight |               |

5. In the Options section, set the following as applicable:
6. On the canvas, add the selected annotation: Click the starting and ending points for the annotation.

| Setting Option   | Description                                                          |
|------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Color            | Color of the annotation objects.                                     |
| Angle            | Angle of the Wire annotation: Orthogonal , Diagonal , or Any Angle . |
| Width            | Width of the Wire annotation.                                        |
| Text             | Text to use for the Callout annotation type.                         |

For ellipses, the starting point is the center of the ellipse.

7. To add more annotations, repeat steps 4 through 6.
8. When you are finished, click OK in the dialog box.

## Ending Design Review Sessions

When you are finished creating reviews or issues, you can end the review session to save the changes. Ending the review session and saving the changes allow other reviewers to see your input. You can also discard all changes made during the current review session and end the review.

This topic describes the two ways to end reviews:

- Saving Changes and Ending Reviews
- Discarding All Changes and Ending Reviews

## Saving Changes and Ending Reviews

To save all changes made and end the review session:

- On the Review Assistant toolbar, click End Review .

<!-- image -->

The new reviews and issues you created during the review session are saved, and the session closes. If automatic review notification was set up, approvers and members are automatically notified by email.

## See Also

- Setting Up Automatic Review Notifications

## Discarding All Changes and Ending Reviews

To discard all changes made during the current review session and end the session:

- On the Review Assistant toolbar, click Discard Review .

<!-- image -->

All reviews and associated issues created during the current review session are discarded, and the session closes.

## Exporting Reviews

You can export specified reviews to an HTML file to view the design review information without having to run the Custom Compiler tool.

## To export reviews:

1. Open the review that you want to export using the Review Manager. See Opening an Existing Review.
2. On the Search Assistant toolbar, click Export Review .

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The Export Design Review to HTML dialog box opens.

<!-- image -->

3. In the Output File box, specify the directory and name for the exported file. If you do not specify a directory, the review data is exported to &lt;current\_working\_directory&gt;/ synopsys\_custom/reports.
4. Select Export Images to export the corresponding images from the review.
5. Select Open in Tab to open the HTML file containing the exported review data in a new tab in the Custom Compiler window.
6. Click OK .

The review data is exported to an HTML file in the default output file directory or in the directory you specified. If you selected Open in Tab, the HTML file opens immediately in a separate tab in the Custom Compiler window.

## Tools for Job Status and Monitoring

This topic describes how to use monitoring tools with Custom Compiler to track and improve the tool performance.

This chapter contains the following topics:

- Job Monitor Tool
- Sentry Monitor Library Tool
- Watchdog Tool

## Job Monitor Tool

Use the Job Monitor to track running job processes.

By default, the Job Monitor tracks batch processes. Interactive process tracking is also available. (See Viewing Running Job Processes).

In addition to using the Job Monitor to track jobs, you can use Tcl preferences to add job classes that combine multiple grid settings into one setting. You can also use Tcl preferences to add job process waiting to allow scripts to finish without interruption.

This topic describes the following:

- Displaying the Job Monitor Tool
- Viewing Running Job Processes
- Applying Job Process Controls
- Managing Job Options
- Filtering Job Groups
- Displaying a Netlist
- Displaying the Output
- Launching a Terminal

<!-- image -->

- Adding Job Classes With xt::createJobClass Tcl
- Adding Job Process Waiting With xt::wait Tcl

## Displaying the Job Monitor Tool

Open the Job Monitor to view current session's batch and interactive processes.

To open the Job Monitor:

- In any design window, choose Tools &gt; Job Monitor .

## Viewing Running Job Processes

You can view job processes as they run with the Job Monitor.

To view a running job process:

1. Begin by opening the Job Monitor Tool. In any design window, choose Tools &gt; Job Monitor .
2. In the Job Monitor, choose View .
3. In the View menu, toggle Job Monitor View Options. The system adds and removes tracking columns as directed.

<!-- image -->

Table 109 describes the Job Monitor view options.

| Option   | Description                                                                           |
|----------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Job      | Displays a tree of job groups and jobs, with leaf nodes for each running application. |

Table 109 Job Monitor View Options

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

| Option          | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-----------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Status          | Displays the status of the process, such as FINISHED, QUEUED, RUNNING, or KILLED. Progress feedback for the job is displayed as a bar graph along with the percentage completed. In addition, the status text is color-coded as follows: ◦ FAILED - bright red ◦ KILLED - dark red ◦ Others - black (default text color) Double-click the status to open the Text Viewer and view associated output files. It also shows the status of the jobs Running, Done, Total (% of Done) while simulation is running for different sections like History, Corners, MonteCarlo, Measurements, and so on. |
| Host            | Name of host associated with this job, with local host noted if the job is running on this system.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| Run Description | Displays the description associated with the job.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| Type            | The job type (group, batch, or interactive).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Creation Time   | Specifies the job creation time.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| Start Time      | Time job was initiated.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| End Time        | Time job ends.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Process ID      | ID as listed on the host.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Queue ID        | The grid identifier associated with the job (only applies if the job was launched via SGE or LSF).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| Output Files    | Expected output files from this job as defined when the job was created.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| %CPU            | CPU usage of the job.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Peak RSS        | Peak resident memory of the job.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| Job Types       | Toggles between the display of batch and interactive jobs.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

4. You can choose to show interactive job processes in addition to batch job processes by choosing View &gt; Job Types , and toggling the Interactive option. Alternatively, use the xtJobMonitorShowInteractiveJobs preference.
5. Choosing File &gt; Close closes the Job Monitor.

## Applying Job Process Controls

You can apply job process controls that suspend, resume, kill, and delete jobs.

To apply job process controls:

1. Begin by opening the Job Monitor Tool. In any design window, choose Tools &gt; Job Monitor .
2. In the Job Monitor, choose Job .
3. Select the job by name. (This step is not required when you are deleting all completed jobs)
4. Choose one of the job process controls.

Table 110 describes the job process controls.

Table 110 Job Process Controls

| Option                                    | Description                                   |
|-------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| Suspend                                   | Halts this process                            |
| Resume                                    | Resumes the halted process                    |
| Kill Selected Jobs                        | Ends this process                             |
| Kill Selected Jobs and All Remaining Jobs | Ends this process and any remaining processes |
| View Output                               | Displays output in the Text Viewer            |
| Delete                                    | Removes this job                              |
| Delete All Completed                      | Removes records of all completed jobs         |

5. Choosing File &gt; Close closes the Job Monitor.

## Managing Job Options

You can manage job options to control batch processing limits, and to optionally set a queue engine. You can optionally specify a job class, which assigns queue engine resources based on a predefined job type.

<!-- image -->

## To manage job options:

1. Begin by opening the Job Monitor Tool. In any design window, choose Tools &gt; Job Monitor .
2. In the Job Monitor, choose File &gt; Options .
3. Choose job management options.

Table 111 describes the job management options.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

| Option    | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-----------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Job Class | Specifies a setting that automatically includes an analysis process, a queue engine, whether concurrent jobs are allowed, and the number of allowable concurrent jobs. CAD Support teams can add custom job classes. For details, see Adding Job Classes With xt::createJobClass Tcl. |

Table 111 Job Management Options

<!-- image -->

## Creating Custom Job Class

PrimeWave has two job classes by default - Simulation and SAEShell. These are defined to simulate within a local host assuming there is no grid available and can allow maximum of 3 and 2 concurrent jobs respectively. In a custom environment, the simulation jobs are usually outsourced to a grid containing machines with high processing capability. Some of the popular Queue Engines supported in PrimeWave Design Environment are SGE, LSF, SLURM, and Network Computer.

To setup a new job class:

1. Click + beside the job class. Add the name of the custom job class you want to add.
2. For a newly added class, select a relevant Queue Engine available in your network. Click Configure to see the additional options related to the selected queue engine. For example, when LSF is selected, the available queues are displayed.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

3. Use the check box to mention the feasible queues to which the simulation job can be submitted. Additional LSF flags and options can be added to the Extra LSF Options field. If the grid machine requires any pre-simulation settings, the complete shell command top prepares the environment before executing the job submit command and can be added to the Setup Command field.
4. The newly created job class appears in the Job Class drop-down menu, sorted alphabetically. To use the job class for the current testbench, select it from Setup &gt; Simulator &gt; Simulation Jobs . The Job Class drop-down displays all available job classes, including the newly added ones. For more information, see .
5. If you want to distribute a job with customized submit command or customized grid protocol, use CUSTOM queue engine to setup the job class. If the environment supports a custom queue engine that is not in the earlier list, you can select CUSTOM

<!-- image -->

in the drop-down menu. The relevant protocol can be chosen from the drop-down menu. The Submit Command can be added to the configuration.

<!-- image -->

## Setting Up Independent Processes Distribution

PrimeWave processes like WaveView, Results Viewer, and Master Calculation Engine can be distributed to a remote grid with an interactive grid job class.

To distribute the processes to remote:

1. Open the Independent Processes Distribution Setup dialog box by selecting Tools &gt; Independent Processes Distribution.
2. Select the Remote (Interactive Grid) option.
3. From the Job Class drop-down, select the existing job class to be used for the remote distribution.
4. If you want to create a new job class to be used for these PrimeWave process, click Job Class Definition to open the Job Definition and Management dialog box for setting up a new job class.

## 5. Click OK .

## Customizing the Job Name

You can customize the job name when launching simulations to the grid engine. The procedure ::sa::run::createJobArrayName should be used to override the default implementation in which the format &lt;testbenchName\_simulatorName&gt; is used for the job name.

<!-- image -->

```
namespace eval ::sa::run { proc createJobArrayName { tb } { set tbName [db::getAttr tb.name] set simName [db::getAttr tb.simulator] return "${tbName}_${simName}" } }
```

## Filtering Job Groups

You can filter jobs that are visible in the Job Monitor, for example, to change from a specific PrimeWave Design Environment session to a more general one. The Job Monitor also remembers the previous filters so you can go back and forth between filtered views.

Select the job group you want to filter from the Filter Job Group menu.

You can also change the current filter to a selected job group by right-clicking on a job group in the job tree and choosing Filter to this job group from the menu.

## Displaying a Netlist

You can display a netlist from the Job Monitor. To display the netlist, select a specific iteration, right-click to display the menu, and choose View Netlist . The netlist opens in the Text Viewer on a new tab.

## Displaying the Output

You can display the output from the Job Monitor. To display the output, select a Job , rightclick to display the menu, and choose View Output . The output log files open in the Text Viewer on a new tab.

## Launching a Terminal

You can launch a terminal from the Job Monitor. To launch a terminal, select a Job , rightclick to display the menu, and choose Launch Terminal . A new terminal opens.

## Adding Job Classes With xt::createJobClass Tcl

You can create job classes that combine settings for individual analysis tools and system environment grids into one setting option.

For example, if you want PrimeSim HSPICE simulation jobs to run on Solaris-64 machines via LSF, and to limit the number of concurrent jobs to 10, you can create a job class that contains these settings.

In use, designers can open the Job Monitor, and select this job class to apply the settings.

This documentation provides two script samples that create custom job classes. To use them, choose the one that most closely matches your requirements, adjust values to create an exact match, and implement the script. You can also write an original script using the supplied Tcl commands and preferences.

This section covers Tcl samples:

- Sample Job Class for Design Rule Checking on Linux Systems
- Sample Job Class for PrimeSim HSPICE Simulation on Solaris Systems

## Sample Job Class for Design Rule Checking on Linux Systems

This Tcl sample configures PrimeSim XA and ICV tool DRC jobs to run on Linux-64 machines via LSF, without limiting the number of concurrent jobs.

You can implement this job class using the sample code that follows.

In use, designers can specify this job class by opening the Job Monitor, choosing File Options , and selecting LSFlinux64 as shown in Figure 57.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

```
# Job Class for Design Rule Checking on Linux Systems# For reference, this sample lists available job class options.# General options: #     JobQueueEngine #     JobLimit #     JobLimitEnabled # LSF-specific options: #     LSFQueues #     LSFResources #     LSFExtraOptions # SGE-specific options: #     SGEProjects #     SGESelectedProject #     SGEExtraOptions # # Configure XA and ICV DRC jobs to run on # linux-64 machines via LSF with no limiting. # set lsflnx [xt::createJobClass LSFlinux64] db::setPrefValue [xt::getJobClassOptionPrefName $lsflnx \ -option "JobQueueEngine"] -value "LSF" db::setPrefValue [xt::getJobClassOptionPrefName $lsflnx \ -option "JobLimitEnabled"] -value false db::setPrefValue [xt::getJobClassOptionPrefName $lsflnx \ -option "LSFResources"] -value "SOL64 0 X86_64 1" xt::addJobClassPrefix XA -jobClass $lsflnx xt::addJobClassPrefix icv_drc -jobClass $lsflnx #
```

Figure 57 Sample Job Class for Design Rule Checking on Linux Systems

## Adding Job Process Waiting With xt::wait Tcl

In Tcl scripts, you can add job process waiting, which blocks user interaction until currently running jobs finish. Job process waiting is useful when your script needs to use the results of any currently running job as input for its next operation.

To add job process waiting to a Tcl script:

1. Identify the job.
- If you created the job using the xt::createJob command, use the returned job object.
- If you want to add waiting to a standard system job process, use the job as listed in the Job Monitor.

To find the job, run the process once using the graphic user interface. Then, in the Job Monitor Job column, take note of the process name.

For example, to add waiting to the IC Compiler export process, choose Export &gt; To ICC , and run the process. In the Job Monitor Job column, note that the Job Monitor identifies the process as dbExportICC .

2. Using the identified job, add the xt::wait command to the Tcl script at the line where you want the script to wait.

In the example that follows, xt::getJobs gets all IC Compiler export jobs. It uses xt::wait to cause the system to wait for these jobs to finish before executing the next Tcl command. While the system waits, it blocks user input. After the jobs finish, the script continues.

The system individually names each job process by appending the underscore character (\_) and adding incremental numbering. For instance, the first dbExportICC

<!-- image -->

```
wildcard character (*) to capture all dbExportICC jobs. # wait for any dbExportICC jobs to finish db::foreach xtJob [xt::getJobs dbExportICC*] { xt::wait $xtJob }
```

<!-- image -->

job is dbExportICC\_1 and the fifteenth is dbExportICC\_15. The example uses the

## 3. Implement your Tcl script.

For details about running Tcl scripts on demand, see Running Tcl Scripts.

For information about making Tcl scripts available from the installation tree, see Defining Startup Settings.

## Sentry Monitor Library Tool

The Sentry Monitor Library is a computer and network monitoring tool that reports error messages for computer and network-related performance issues while you are running a Synopsys software product.

[See Synopsys Sentry Monitor Library Error Messages.](https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com/s/article/Synopsys-Sentry-Monitor-Library-Error-Messages)

## Note:

You must be logged in to SolvNetPlus for the earlier link to connect directly to the article. If you are prompted to log in to SolvNetPlus upon clicking the link to the article, log in, click the link again to reach the article.

The Sentry Monitor Library monitors and reports the following types of issues:

- High CPU use (host and processes)
- High memory use (physical memory, cache, and swap)
- Poor network conditions (packet transmission issues, host latency)

## Watchdog Tool

The Watchdog tool provides information to assist Design and CAD teams in analyzing tool usage and quality for their users. The main functionality of the Watchdog tool is to collect statistical information about Custom Compiler sessions. This version of the Watchdog tool can also copy Custom Compiler log files (only software failures or all logs) to a central location. By dividing the total session open time by the number of failures, you can calculate the failure rate of the Custom Compiler tool. This data can also be used to analyze common failures and work with your Synopsys representative to determine root causes and resolve them more quickly. Overall, the Watchdog tool can help increase the stability of the Custom Compiler tool.

<!-- image -->

The Watchdog tool uses the process ID of the Custom Compiler session. It is attached to the Custom Compiler session and starts a collection of statistics and machine information.

The Watchdog tool writes the collected data into a database and copies the log file after the session is ended.

The collection of statistics and copying of log files can be configured in the Watchdog config file.

<!-- image -->

This topic describes the following:

- Installing the Watchdog Tool
- Watchdog Outputs
- Watchdog Report Statistics

## Installing the Watchdog Tool

To install the Watchdog tool:

1. Create a directory to collect all watchdog statistic data including log files.

## Note:

All users should have read-write access to the created directory.

The directory should be available to all users and from all machines (that is, a shared location).

## 2. Add the following environment variable:

## bash:

export SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_WATCHDOG\_DIR=&lt;Directory from 1st step&gt;

<!-- image -->

```
csh: setenv SYNOPSYS_CUSTOM_WATCHDOG_DIR <Directory from 1st step>
```

3. Create a watchdog.cfg configuration file in the $SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_WATCHDOG\_DIR directory.

The configuration file should contain the following:

```
[Watchdog] collectStatistics = True/False collectLogs = True/False collectNonCrashLogs = True/False
```

The preceding options control the following features of the Watchdog tool:

- collectStatistics - Enables collection of statistical data in the $SYNOPSYS\_CUSTOM\_WATCHDOG\_DIR/data.sqlite database.
- collectLogs - Enables copying of software failure logs only into the Watchdog statistics directory (from step 2).
- collectNonCrashLogs - Works with the collectLogs option and enables copying non-failure logs, as well.

The Watchdog tool runs in the background for each Custom Compiler session after you complete the preceding installation procedure.

## Watchdog Outputs

The Watchdog tool saves all statistical information into a database and copies log files into a central location. Both features can be disabled and enabled in the configuration file.

## Database

The Watchdog tool collects all statistic information for all users in one SqLite database named data.sqlite .

## Database Structure

Statistics data for each version of the Custom Compiler tool is collected in separate tables in the database.

Each table has the following columns:

- Maximum RAM and Virtual Memory usage
- CPU Time for parent and children processes (children processes are external processes run via the Custom Compiler tool)

- User usage time based on command execution frequency
- Start and End Times (Real time)
- Crash stack and exit code
- Copied log file location (nothing if feature disabled)
- Machine information:
- Total RAM
- Total Swap
- CPU count
- Platform
- User information:
- User ID
- User Group
- Tool version information:
- Tool name
- Config number

## Database example:

<!-- image -->

## Log Files

All copied log files can be found in the root logs directory located in the Watchdog output directory. The log files are copied into yyyy/month/dd directories corresponding to the date of copy.

## Log directory example:

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

```
|     |  +-<copied log files> |     +-29 |        +-<copied log files> +-2023 +-Jan |  +-04 |  |  +-<copied log files> |  +-08 |  |  +-<copied log files> |  +-21 |     +-<copied log files> +-Feb +-01 +-<copied log files>
```

## Watchdog Report Statistics

The wreport.py utility can be used to generate high-level report from watchdog database. It is in the watchdog directory (for example, &lt;CC install dir&gt;/auxx/watchdog/ wreport.py ).

The usage of the utility is the following:

```
wreport.py [-r <release name>] -d <database location> Use -h(--help) for help.
```

If the release option is not set, the utility reports for all existing releases.

The following is a simple example of wreport.py output:

```
<Release name> Total Sessions   : 97 Crashed Sessions : 6 Unique Crashes   : 4 Users            : 7 CPU Time         : 4.865 hours of cpu usage Elapsed Time     : 117.879 hours tool was up Usage Time       : 4.745 hours tool actively used MTBC             : 0.791 hours (Usage Time / Crashed Sessions) Longest Session  : 0.783 hours across all sessions : 0.029 hours across crashed sessions Shortest Session : 0.000 hours across all sessions : 0.000 hours across crashed sessions Average Session  : 0.049 hours across all sessions : 0.012 hours across crashed sessions
```

## Query on Database

If the report generated by the wreport.py does not provide enough information, you can use database queries for get more information.

<!-- image -->

You can get more database info using the following methods:

- sqlite3 Command
- List the Tables
- Convert Database
- Number of Sessions

## sqlite3 Command

Use the sqlite3 command:

```
sqlite3 [OPTIONS] database [SQL Commands]
```

## List the Tables

data.sqlite can contain several tables which are corresponding to the versions of the Custom Compiler tool.

To list the names of the tables you can use the following command:

```
sqlite3 data.sqlite "SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table'"
```

Choose the version you want and do the query on it.

## Convert Database

Sqlite3 allows you to format the output. The useful formats are CSV and HTML.

Use the following command to convert data.sqlite to CSV:

```
sqlite3 -header -csv data.sqlite "SELECT * FROM '<table name>'" > {output}
```

## Number of Sessions

Use the following command to get the number of overall sessions for the version of the Custom Compiler tool:

```
sqlite3 data.sqlite "SELECT count(*) FROM '<table name>'"
```

Use the following command to get the number of crashed sessions:

```
sqlite3 data.sqlite "SELECT count(*) FROM '<table name>' WHERE ExitCode <> 'None' AND ExitCode <> 0"
```

## Customizing the Software and Workspaces

The Custom Compiler environment provides ways for you to customize the user interface to meet your requirements and preferences. For example, you can pin tabs or define Custom workspaces to retain the arrangement of tabs, toolbars, assistants, and canvas. You can also configure the graphical user interface and add dialog boxes.

This chapter contains the following topics:

- Defining Custom Workspaces
- Configuring Custom Windows
- Creating Dialog Boxes
- Adding Assistants and Other User Interfaces Using Tcl/Tk
- Tcl Sample for Custom Graphic User Interface

## Defining Custom Workspaces

You can define Custom workspaces to retain the arrangement of tabs, toolbars, assistants, and canvas. Different workspaces allow users with varying requirements and preferences to work from the same computer.

These sections cover:

- About Custom Workspaces
- Creating Workspaces
- Saving Workspaces
- Loading Workspaces
- Switching to Another Workspace
- Renaming Workspaces

<!-- image -->

- Deleting Workspaces
- Preserving Workspace Geometries

## About Custom Workspaces

Custom workspaces preserve arrangements you make to the menus, toolbars, and assistants of a window type. Window types are editor and manager windows, such as the Layout Editor and Library Manager.

Multiple workspaces can be made for the design editors, allowing you to customize design sessions to your preference. During a design session, you can choose which workspace to display at any given time.

For example, you can set up a schematic window with the toolbar and assistant arrangement preferred for schematic editing. You can control the size and positions of all schematics as they open.

After arranging the workspace, you can save it using the Window &gt; Workspaces menu. Changes to an active workspace are preserved when closing active sessions.

<!-- image -->

In the Manage Workspaces dialog box, you can save an XML file containing the workspace definition. You can load the XML file to restore a missing workspace or to modify an existing workspace.

The layout and schematic windows provide default workspaces that you can modify and save as custom workspaces. Default workspaces are also available for work in SDL and templates. Although you cannot customize the SDL and template workspaces, these workspaces will remember your setup between sessions.

You can save a custom window you have defined as a custom workspace. To define a custom window, see Configuring Custom Windows.

<!-- image -->

## Creating Workspaces

You can create workspaces to present a consistent user interface for design from one session to the next session.

To create a custom workspace:

1. In a Custom Compiler session, open a design, and position windows, toolbars, and assistants in the preferred arrangement.
2. Choose Window &gt; Workspaces &gt; New .
3. In the New Workspace dialog box, type a name for this new workspace.
4. (Optional) Select Set as Default for Schematic Editor windows or Set as Default for Layout Editor windows to make this workspace configuration the default for the window type.
5. Click Create .

<!-- image -->

The workspace name is added to the Window &gt; Workspaces menu.

Changes to the workspace are automatically saved when closing designs. To save your workspace as an XML file, see Saving Workspaces.

## Saving Workspaces

Save a custom workspace so that it is available across different design sessions, and to retain modifications made in this session.

To save a workspace:

1. Choose Window &gt; Workspaces &gt; Manage .
2. In the Manage Workspaces dialog box, select the workspaces to save.
3. Choose , or click
4. File &gt; Save Save .
4. In the Select File to Save Workspace(s) dialog box, type the name of the file in which to save the workspaces. The system saves workspace files in the XML format.
5. Click Save .

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Loading Workspaces

Important: Make sure that the workspace you are loading is created and displayed in the Manage Workspaces dialog box.

To load a workspace:

1. Choose Window &gt; Workspaces &gt; Manage .

The Manage Workspaces dialog box opens and lists the available workspaces and the corresponding window types.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

2. Choose File &gt; Load , or click Load
3. In the Select Workspace File to Open dialog box, locate and select the workspace (.xml) file.
4. Click Open .

## Switching to Another Workspace

Important: If you do not see the workspace you want to display, try loading it first. See Loading Workspaces.

To switch to another workspace:

- Choose Window &gt; Workspaces &gt; &lt;workspace\_name&gt;.

A check mark next to the workspace name indicates that the workspace is displayed.

<!-- image -->

## Renaming Workspaces

All workspaces except the default workspaces are available for renaming.

To rename a workspace:

1. Choose Window &gt; Workspaces &gt; Manage .
2. Select the workspace name, and then choose Edit &gt; Rename .
3. Type a unique name for the workspace.
4. Press Enter.

## Deleting Workspaces

Delete a custom workspace to remove it from your list of workspaces.

## Caution:

You cannot undo this operation. Workspaces that have not been saved to an XML file cannot be retrieved.

To delete a workspace:

1. Choose Window &gt; Workspaces &gt; Manage .
2. In the Manage Workspace(s) dialog box, select the workspaces you want to delete.
3. Choose Edit &gt; Delete , or click Delete

<!-- image -->

.

To retrieve a deleted workspace from an XML file, see Loading Workspaces.

## Preserving Workspace Geometries

You can preserve the size and position of a window of your current session in a future session in the following cases:

- The Window tabs are disabled.
- The Window tabs are enabled and the current window is the only window in the frame.

For example, the you can configure the window geometry of the Search and Replace dialog box (without a frame) with your current window and save this geometry for future sessions.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Further, if the Layout Editor and Schematic Editor windows are opened in separate frames in the SDL flow, you can configure the window geometries and save these for future sessions.

<!-- image -->

To open the Layout Editor and Schematic Editor windows in separate frames, set the lxOpenInNewFrames and lxAutoArrangeWindows Tcl preferences to true , as shown in the following example:

```
db::setPrefValue lxOpenInNewFrames -value true db::setPrefValue lxAutoArrangeWindows -value true
```

To preserve the window geometries in a future session:

- Choose File &gt; Quit from the Home tab. The Exit dialog box opens. Select Display Resources check box and click Exit .

<!-- image -->

## Configuring Custom Windows

You can configure custom windows to create an environment with preferred menu and toolbar options for a specific type of designing. For example, you can create a new menu or toolbar that contains all the commands that you frequently use.

This topic describes the following:

- Planning the Custom Windows
- Creating Custom Windows
- Creating New Custom Menus and Toolbars
- Adding Commands in Custom Menus and Toolbars
- Deleting Menus, Menu Commands, and Toolbars
- Saving Custom Windows for Future Sessions

## Planning the Custom Windows

Plan the custom window as follows:

1. For the type of custom window you want to create, open a design, and evaluate the current user interface. You can create a custom window for any window that contains menus and toolbars, including the Console.
2. Make a list of the items you want to add, move, and delete.
- You can create new menus on menu bars and populate them with commands from a list of available operations called actions .
- You can add new menu commands to existing menus from the list of available actions.
- You can move menus and toolbars to different locations within the window.
- You can delete menus, individual commands, and toolbars from the window.

## Creating Custom Windows

Before you start to add menus and toolbars, you must first create a new custom window. This is the window that will contain the custom menus, toolbars, and dialog boxes that you will be adding.

<!-- image -->

To create a new custom window:

1. In the design editor, choose Window &gt; Customize . The Customize Window dialog box opens.

<!-- image -->

The system freezes all menus, toolbars, and assistants so that you can manipulate the menus and toolbars. For example, you can select and display a menu, but you cannot use it.

2. Do one of the following:
- Creating New Custom Menus and Toolbars
- Adding Commands in Custom Menus and Toolbars
- Deleting Menus, Menu Commands, and Toolbars

## Creating New Custom Menus and Toolbars

Based on the plan you created in Planning the Custom Windows, you can create new menus and toolbars in the custom window.

To create a new menu or toolbar:

1. In the custom window you just created, right-click the menu bar, and choose Create Menu or Create Toolbar .
2. In the Create Menu or Create Toolbar dialog box, type the name of the new menu or toolbar.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

3. Click Create . The new menu name appears on the menu bar. If you created a new toolbar, the new toolbar appears below the set of existing toolbars, but it does not have a name.
4. Continue by developing the custom window as designed.
5. Choose one of the following:
- Adding Commands in Custom Menus and Toolbars
- Deleting Menus, Menu Commands, and Toolbars
- Saving Custom Windows for Future Sessions

<!-- image -->

## Adding Commands in Custom Menus and Toolbars

Based on the plan you created in Planning the Custom Windows, you can add commands in the custom menu or toolbar you just created.

To add new commands in a menu:

1. In the Customize Window dialog box, choose a category. The list of available actions (or commands) for that category appears.

For example, if you choose the Design category, the list of design actions appears. The actions are commands that you can add to the menu you created.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

2. (Optional) To filter the list shown, type the action name in the Filter box.
3. To add a command, drag the action (command) to the newly created menu or toolbar. The command appears in the menu or on the toolbar.

The following example shows that the Design &gt; Summary command is added to the newly created menu called MyNewMenu.

<!-- image -->

The following example shows that the Tool Help, Create Via (icon), Display Resource Editor (icon), and Layout Display Options commands are added to the nameless custom toolbar.

<!-- image -->

4. (Optional) If you have more than one command in the custom menu or toolbar, reposition the command by dragging it to a new position.
5. (Optional) To add a line separator between commands, right-click where you want to add the separator, and choose Add Separator .
6. (Optional) To delete a command, right-click the command, and choose Remove .

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

7. Continue by developing the custom window as designed.
8. Choose one of the following:
- Deleting Menus, Menu Commands, and Toolbars
- Saving Custom Windows for Future Sessions
- Creating New Custom Menus and Toolbars

## Deleting Menus, Menu Commands, and Toolbars

You can delete menus, menu commands, and toolbars in your custom window as follows:

- To delete an entire menu or toolbar, right-click the menu or toolbar, and choose Remove .
- To remove a menu command, right-click the command, and choose Remove .
- To remove all custom menus and toolbars, in the Customize Window dialog box, click Defaults .

## Saving Custom Windows for Future Sessions

You can save custom windows for this session only or for future sessions. To keep the custom window only for this session, do nothing more. The custom settings will end when the session ends.

To save the custom window for future sessions:

1. In the Customize Window dialog box, click Close to exit the frozen user interface state.
2. Create a new workspace. See Creating Workspaces.

<!-- image -->

## Creating a Basic Dialog Box

Create a basic dialog box by adding the dialog box widget to your Tcl script.

You can visualize dialog box appearance by entering the Tcl for the dialog box, and all of its widget elements, directly in the Console. When you are done, you can copy the Tcl to your script for implementation.

To create a dialog box:

1. Add a Tcl procedure to create a graphic user interface, for example proc showImportSPICE {} {} .
2. Add the Tcl command gi::createDialog at the top of the Tcl procedure.

By default, dialog boxes show Help and Close buttons, only. This dialog box format is useful for showing messages. The user reads the message, and can choose to either click the Help button or close the dialog box.

To transform the default dialog box into one that executes a Tcl procedure, add the -execProc argument, and give it the name of a Tcl procedure to execute. Adding the -execProc argument adds OK , Apply , and Cancel buttons.

If you do not plan to provide access to Help, add the -showHelp argument, and set it to false .

If you want to render the dialog box as invisible, add the -shown argument, and set it to false .

Example 6 creates a dialog box with the title Import Spice Subckt File .

## Example 6 Dialog Box

3. Choose an option:
- Continue to create the dialog box sample by adding a tab group to contain Main and Options tabs. See next Creating Tab Groups.
- Add elements to the dialog box. See Creating Elements for Collecting Input.

## Creating Mutually Exclusive Input

Create a mutually exclusive widget in a dialog box when you want to allow the selection of only one of many possible, mutually exclusive values. You can render this widget as either a set of radio buttons or a single combo box.

Example 11 adds two mutex input boxes where the user can select only one of the available options in each.

To create a mutually exclusive input widget:

1. Add the Tcl command gi::createMutexInput .

Example 11 adds two mutex input widgets. The first widget offers the option to set a pin type. The second widget offers the alternate, and mutually exclusive option to set a pin direction.

## Example 11 Mutex Input Widget

```
set outputPinType [gi::createMutexInput outputPinType \ -parent $subOptions -label "Type:" -enum {input \ output inputOutput} -viewType combo] set outputPinDirection [gi::createMutexInput \ outputPinDirection -parent $subOptions -label "Side:" \ -enum {left right top bottom} -viewType combo]
```

## Creating Splitter Groups

Create a splitter group in a dialog box when you want to offer the ability to change the relative sizes of widgets.

To create a splitter group:

- Add the Tcl command gi::createSplitterGroup .

Example 16 adds horizontal and vertical splitters in a dialog box. The dialog box includes two List Input widgets (whose horizontal size can be changed relative to each other) and a Table widget (whose vertical size can be changed relative to the List Input widgets).

## Example 16 Splitter Group Widget

```
set dialog [gi::createDialog myDialog -title "Splitter"] set spv [gi::createSplitterGroup splitv -parent $dialog \ -orientation vertical]
```

<!-- image -->

```
set sph [gi::createSplitterGroup splith -parent $spv ] gi::createListInput ll -parent $sph -viewType list \ -items {A B C} gi::createListInput rl -parent $sph -viewType list -items item1 set table [gi::createTable table -parent $spv \ -allowAddRows true] gi::createColumn  -parent $table -stretch true
```

<!-- image -->

The following commands specify the geometry of the dialog box and the vertical size of the List Input and Table widgets.

```
db::setAttr dialog.geometry -value 500x300 db::setAttr spv.childSizes -value {160 80}
```

To resize the dialog box vertically without changing the vertical sizes of the List Input widgets, use this command:

```
db::setAttr spv.childStretchFactors -value {0 1}
```

Create a push button widget in a dialog box when you want to add a stateless button that performs a single operation. Push button widgets align with labeled inputs, and do not expand in either the horizontal or vertical direction.

## Creating Elements that Reconfigure

Create elements that reconfigure when you want to guide the user to a targeted choice from a larger set of information. You can create tables, and dynamic lists, which adjust in response to user interaction. These elements save space, and show only the information you designate.

## These sections cover:

- Creating Tables
- Creating Dynamic Lists

## Creating Tables

Create a table in a dialog box when you want to offer graphic arrangement in which each cell can contain data or an additional widget. You can choose to represent the table in standard format or as a tree where the parent of a row object is another row.

<!-- image -->

Tables are labeled widgets, and they expand both horizontally and vertically.

To create a table:

- Add the Tcl command gi::createTable .

## See Also

- Sample GUI for Creating a Symbol from a SPICE Netlist

## Creating Dynamic Lists

Create a dynamic list in a dialog box when you want offer a list in which the user can add or remove entries. The input value of a dynamic list is taken from the items which have been specified. Dynamic lists are labeled widgets, and expand both horizontally and vertically. Clicking on any item changes the item to an editable field. Erasing a name removes the row. Clicking on Click to Add adds an additional row.

To create a dynamic list:

```
► Add the Tcl command gi::createDynamicList .
```

## See Also

- Sample GUI for Creating a Symbol from a SPICE Netlist

## Adjusting Custom Dialog Box Layouts

Adjust dialog box layouts to arrange the elements in proper relationship to each other.

For example, the standard usage sequence for a dialog box progresses from left to right, and top to bottom. By default. However, dialog box creation adds each element in a vertical arrangement from top to bottom, and not from left to right. Adjust the layout to display the best suggested usage sequence from left to right in addition to top to bottom.

To arrange a dialog box layout:

- Add the Tcl gi::layout .

Example 17 adjusts the arrangement of the two input fields from stacked to side by side.

```
Example 17 Adjusting Layouts gi::layout $outputPinType -rightOf $outputPinRegExp gi::layout $outputPinDirection -rightOf $outputPinType
```

<!-- image -->
